## #48: Backcasting steering-as-attack detection: can a monitor flag when a model has been maliciously steered? (Score: 4.38)

**ID:** gen-1572

**Research Question:** Can a lightweight monitor reliably detect, from activation statistics alone, when an open model's forward pass has been tampered with by a malicious steering vector? How does detection accuracy trade off against steering magnitude and false-positive rate on clean inputs?

**Approach:** On an open 7B model, generate two populations of forward passes over a fixed prompt set: clean (no steering) and steered (a malicious direction, e.g., a 'comply with harmful request' vector, injected at varying magnitudes). Collect simple activation statistics per layer (norms, per-dimension means/variances, distances from the clean running mean). Train a lightweight anomaly detector (e.g., a one-class detector or small logistic classifier) on clean activations and evaluate whether it flags steered passes. Sweep steering magnitude to get a detection-AUROC-vs-magnitude curve and report the false-positive rate on held-out clean inputs. Inference plus a tiny detector — minimal compute on a single GPU.

**Experiments:** - Build the clean-vs-steered activation dataset: collect per-layer activation summaries for ~500 clean and ~500 steered generations at one steering magnitude. Measure separability via a simple t-SNE/PCA visualization and a held-out classifier. Expected outcome: visible/measurable separation at moderate-to-large magnitudes.
- Sweep steering magnitude across ~5 levels and plot detection AUROC vs magnitude, fixing a false-positive budget (e.g., 5% on clean inputs). Measure the magnitude threshold above which detection is reliable (AUROC > 0.9). Expected outcome: a detectability curve identifying how 'loud' an attack must be to be caught.
- Stress-test generalization: train the detector on one steering direction and test on a different (unseen) malicious direction. Measure cross-direction AUROC. Expected outcome: partial generalization, indicating whether the monitor learns a generic tamper signature or is direction-specific.

**Impact Chain:** If activation-statistics monitors can flag malicious steering, then defenders running open-weight models can add a cheap tamper-detection layer against an emerging attack vector where adversaries inject steering vectors to bypass safety. This builds toward long-horizon safer-monitoring infrastructure, reducing the catastrophic-risk pathway in which open models are silently steered into harmful behavior at deployment scale without operators noticing.

**Strength Rationale:** Counterfactual value is 5: this is neglected, long-horizon (>1yr threat model) monitoring infrastructure built entirely on open weights with no lab access. With 5s on narrow scope and low compute, the deliverable is a single tightly-scoped detection study (AUROC vs steering magnitude plus false-positive rate) that a beginner team can complete and write up in 30 hours.

**Alternative Framings:** Reframe as a benchmark contribution: release the clean-vs-steered activation dataset and a baseline detector so others can compete on tamper-detection AUROC.

## #49: Probing-Classifier Confound Audit Tool (Score: 4.38)

**ID:** gen-1668

**Research Question:** When a linear probe achieves high accuracy on a safety-relevant concept, is it reading the concept or a surface confound (token frequency, length, topic)? Can we package a standard 'probe sanity suite' that tells a newcomer how much of their probe's accuracy is genuine concept signal?

**Approach:** Using TransformerLens to extract activations from a small open model, train a target probe for a safety-relevant concept (e.g., 'refusal-worthy request'). Then automatically train a battery of control probes: on shuffled labels (a la Hewitt & Liang control tasks), on a bag-of-tokens baseline, and on identified confounds (length, topic). Report a selectivity score = probe accuracy minus control-task accuracy, plus the gap against each baseline. Wrap this into a small reusable library that takes (activations, labels) and emits a diagnostic report. Inference plus linear probes on a small model — single consumer GPU, a few hours.

**Experiments:** - Implement the core suite on one concept dataset: train target probe + shuffled-label control + bag-of-tokens baseline, and compute selectivity. Measure target accuracy vs control accuracy. Expected outcome: a working tool that outputs a selectivity score and flags when a probe is no better than a token baseline.
- Add confound probes (length, topic) and run on a 'refusal-worthy request' dataset. Measure how much of the target probe's accuracy is recoverable from confounds alone. Expected outcome: quantification of how much apparent concept-detection is explained by surface confounds (hypothesis: a non-trivial fraction).
- Demonstrate a false-positive catch: deliberately construct a confounded dataset (concept correlated with length) and show the suite flags low selectivity even at high raw accuracy. Measure raw accuracy vs selectivity on this adversarial case. Expected outcome: the tool correctly warns 'this probe is reading a confound', validating its utility.

**Impact Chain:** Probing is the gateway method underlying many proposed safety monitors (e.g., 'we can detect deception with a probe'). If probes silently read confounds, such monitors give false assurance. A confound-audit tool prevents over-claimed detection results from propagating, reducing the catastrophic-risk pathway where a deployed safety monitor based on a confounded probe fails to catch the dangerous behavior it was trusted to flag.

**Strength Rationale:** Counterfactual value is 5: it packages interpretability best-practice into a reusable, lab-free tool that labs underprioritize, usable entirely on open models. With 5s on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute, the deliverable is a single well-bounded probe-sanity suite with a concrete selectivity-score output, ideal for a beginner team's first project in 30 hours.

**Alternative Framings:** Frame as a checklist + leaderboard: audit several published 'probe detects X' safety claims and report each one's selectivity, turning the tool into a meta-evaluation of probe-based monitors.

## #50: Length-Bias Reward Hacking Across Open Reward Models (Score: 4.38)

**ID:** gen-1885

**Research Question:** How universal and how strong is verbosity bias across publicly available open reward models? When two responses are matched in content but differ only in length, how often does each reward model prefer the longer one?

**Approach:** Collect a panel of public open reward models (several from RewardBench / HuggingFace). Build matched response pairs that are identical in substantive content but differ in length by padding one with on-topic, content-free elaboration. Score each pair with every reward model and record how often the longer response is preferred. Produce a comparative 'verbosity susceptibility' leaderboard with confidence intervals, and check whether padding style (filler vs restatement) changes the effect. Inference-only on reward models — minimal compute on a single GPU.

**Experiments:** - Build the matched-pair set: take ~100 prompts with a base response, then create a length-padded variant per response that adds no new content. Validate via human spot-check that padding adds length but not quality. Expected outcome: a clean matched-pair dataset isolating length from content.
- Score all pairs with one reward model to establish the pipeline and measure its longer-preferred rate with CIs. Expected outcome: a reproducible per-model verbosity-preference rate above 50% (the bias).
- Run the full panel of reward models and rank them into a verbosity-susceptibility leaderboard with bootstrap CIs. Measure spread across models. Expected outcome: a comparative leaderboard showing which open reward models are most and least length-biased.

**Impact Chain:** Reward-model misspecification is a core RLHF open problem; verbosity bias is a concrete, measurable instance that propagates into deployed models as sycophantic padding and reward hacking. A public cross-model audit gives RLHF practitioners reusable infrastructure to pick less length-biased reward models. This reduces the catastrophic-risk pathway where optimization against a biased reward model systematically degrades model honesty/quality at scale across many downstream RLHF pipelines.

**Strength Rationale:** Counterfactual value is 5: an open, comparative audit of public reward models is reusable safety infrastructure that labs underinvest in, needing only inference and no training data. With 5s on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute, it is a single matched-pair audit with a clear leaderboard deliverable and explicit success criteria, completable by a beginner team in 30 hours.

**Alternative Framings:** Reframe as a 'reward-model debiasing benchmark': release the matched-pair set as a standard probe so new reward models can report their verbosity-susceptibility score.

**Approach:** Take a public open-weight EM organism (from 'Model Organisms for Emergent Misalignment', arXiv:2506.11613, or Betley et al.). Optionally probe whether quantization noise interacts with the misaligned-persona direction (e.g., by checking if 4-bit destabilizes or partially suppresses it). Fully inference-only on a single consumer GPU, a few hours.

**Experiments:** - Reproduce the fp16 baseline: run the misalignment battery on the public EM organism at full precision and record misaligned-answer rate and coherence. Expected outcome: a baseline matching the organism's published misalignment level.
- Run the same battery at 8-bit and 4-bit and measure the change in misaligned-answer rate and coherence vs fp16, with confidence intervals. Expected outcome: a precision-vs-misalignment curve showing whether quantization meaningfully shifts safety behavior (in either direction).
- Probe the mechanism: compare a coherence-vs-misalignment scatter across precisions to see whether 4-bit reduces misalignment mainly by degrading coherence (incidental) or independently. Expected outcome: evidence on whether any quantization effect is a genuine safety shift or an artifact of degraded fluency.

**Impact Chain:** Most real open-weight usage is quantized, but safety evaluations are typically run at full precision. If quantization changes misalignment severity, then full-precision evals do not reflect how models actually behave in the wild. Surfacing this deployment-relevant variable warns evaluators to test at deployment precision. This reduces the catastrophic-risk pathway where a model judged acceptably safe at fp16 behaves more dangerously (or is wrongly assumed safe) once quantized and deployed on consumer hardware at scale.

**Strength Rationale:** Counterfactual value is 5: it surfaces a deployment-relevant variable that labs running full precision rarely test, using only public model organisms and inference, no lab infrastructure. With 5s on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute, it is a single clean experiment (misalignment vs precision) with explicit success criteria, executable by a beginner team on a single consumer GPU within 30 hours.

**Alternative Framings:** Reframe as a general 'deployment-realism' eval audit: treat quantization as one of several deployment-time transforms (quantization, KV-cache, sampling temperature) and report which most perturb measured safety.

**Cited Sources:** 'Model Organisms for Emergent Misalignment' (arXiv:2506.11613) — releases the open-weight EM organism evaluated across precisions.; Betley et al. — original emergent-misalignment work and organisms providing the standard misalignment battery.; 'The Rogue Scalpel' (arXiv:2509.22067) — shows activation noise affects refusal, motivating the quantization-as-noise hypothesis.

## #53: Relearning-Resistance Stress Test: A Public Benchmark for Unlearning Robustness on a Single GPU (Score: 4.38)

**ID:** gen-2070

**Research Question:** Can a lightweight, standardized stress test let anyone verify in an afternoon whether an 'unlearned' open model has truly removed dangerous knowledge or merely hidden it, by measuring how easily that knowledge is recovered through small-scale relearning attacks?

**Approach:** Build a small, shareable harness. Either start from a publicly available unlearned checkpoint, or apply RMU yourself (public code) to a base model on a tiny WMDP-style forget set so you control the unlearning. Then run a fixed battery of relearning attacks: fine-tune on 5, 20, and 50 benign-but-topically-adjacent examples; paraphrase probing; and few-shot elicitation. After each attack, re-measure forget-set accuracy and plot a recovery curve (accuracy vs number of relearning examples). Summarize each model with a single 'fragility score' (e.g., area under the recovery curve, or accuracy recovered after 50 examples relative to the pre-unlearning model). Everything -- RMU, tiny fine-tunes, and inference eval -- fits on a single consumer GPU in a few hours, and the harness is packaged so others can drop in a checkpoint and get a fragility score.

**Experiments:** - Reproduce a clean unlearning baseline: apply RMU to a small open model on a tiny WMDP-style forget set and confirm forget-set accuracy drops to near-chance while retain-set accuracy stays high. Measure: forget-set and retain-set accuracy pre/post unlearning. Expected outcome: a checkpoint that looks properly unlearned, providing the starting point for attacks.
- Run the relearning-by-fine-tuning attack at 5/20/50 benign-adjacent examples and plot the recovery curve. Measure: forget-set accuracy after each relearning budget. Expected outcome: substantial knowledge recovery from as few as 5-20 examples, confirming relearning fragility and producing the curve that defines the fragility score.
- Run the non-fine-tuning attacks (paraphrase probing, few-shot elicitation) on the same unlearned checkpoint and compare their recovery to the fine-tuning attacks. Measure: accuracy recovered by each attack type. Expected outcome: fine-tuning recovers the most knowledge, but paraphrase/few-shot attacks recover a nontrivial amount with zero weight updates, showing the harness catches multiple fragility modes.

**Impact Chain:** If a turnkey fragility score makes fake unlearning trivially detectable, then the community and auditors can reject 'unlearned' models whose hazardous knowledge resurfaces after a handful of relearning examples -> only genuinely robust unlearning passes as safe -> this closes the misuse pathway where a model certified as having forgotten bioweapon/cyber knowledge is quietly restored to full capability by a user with minimal fine-tuning data.

**Strength Rationale:** It scores maximally on counterfactual value, narrow scope, and low compute: robust unlearning auditing is fuzzy, hard-to-do-well safety work that labs deprioritize and that needs no proprietary data, and it ships a single reusable harness with one summary metric. The deliverable (fragility score + recovery curve) gives an explicit, self-contained success criterion grounded in a peer-reviewed ICML result on relearning vulnerability.

**Alternative Framings:** Reframe as a comparative audit: instead of one harness, run the stress test across several publicly released unlearned checkpoints/methods and publish a ranked robustness leaderboard so the community can see which unlearning methods actually resist relearning.

**Cited Sources:** Fan et al. (arXiv:2502.05374, ICML 2025) -- shows SOTA unlearning is recoverable from a few relearning points; motivates the relearning-attack battery and fragility score; WMDP (arXiv:2403.03218) -- public hazardous-knowledge benchmark providing the forget-set content; RMU (public implementation) -- enables applying a standard unlearning method on a tiny forget set on one GPU

## #54: StrongREJECT Scoring Replicated Across Open Judge Models (Score: 4.38)

**ID:** gen-211

**Research Question:** How much do attack-success-rate (ASR) measurements from the StrongREJECT jailbreak benchmark depend on which judge model does the scoring, and how well do different open judge models agree when scoring the same fixed set of jailbreak transcripts?

**Approach:** Take a fixed corpus of jailbreak attempt transcripts (prompt + model response pairs spanning successful and failed jailbreaks) -- either the released StrongREJECT examples or a fixed set generated once and frozen. Apply the published StrongREJECT scoring rubric using several different open judge models (varying family and size) as the grader, holding the rubric and prompt constant. Compute inter-judge agreement (e.g., Krippendorff's alpha / Cohen's kappa on the binarized verdicts, plus correlation on the continuous scores) and the resulting ASR each judge reports for each attack method. The twist is swapping the judge while freezing transcripts, isolating judge variance from attack variance. This is inference-only scoring; the only cost is running several open judges over a fixed transcript set, which fits a single GPU in a few hours.

**Experiments:** - Assemble and freeze the transcript corpus and score it with one reference open judge using the StrongREJECT rubric. Measure: per-method ASR under the reference judge. Expected outcome: ASR numbers roughly consistent with published StrongREJECT results, validating the scoring pipeline.
- Score the identical frozen transcripts with 3-5 additional open judge models and compute pairwise inter-judge agreement. Measure: Krippendorff's alpha / kappa and score correlation across judges. Expected outcome: only moderate agreement, with systematic disagreement concentrated on borderline (partial-compliance) transcripts.
- Quantify how judge choice shifts the headline ASR per attack method. Measure: spread (max - min) of reported ASR across judges for each attack method. Expected outcome: ASR can swing by a meaningful margin depending solely on the judge, showing that reported jailbreak success rates are judge-dependent and need a fixed judge to be comparable.

**Impact Chain:** If ASR depends substantially on the judge, then jailbreak-robustness claims across papers and red-team reports are not comparable unless the judge is fixed -> the field adopts judge-standardized reporting and treats judge variance as a known error bar -> this hardens the adversarial-robustness measurement stack that gates whether a model is deemed safe to deploy, reducing the risk that an unsafe model is mistakenly certified jailbreak-resistant because of a lenient judge.

**Strength Rationale:** It scores maximally on counterfactual value and narrow scope: third-party scrutiny of a widely used safety metric is exactly the kind of open-infrastructure work external researchers can do but labs rarely prioritize, and it is a single clean statistical experiment (inter-judge agreement + ASR spread) with an explicit success criterion. Freezing transcripts cleanly isolates the variable of interest, making the result unambiguous and reproducible.

**Alternative Framings:** Reframe as a robustness-of-rankings study: instead of focusing on absolute ASR, test whether the *ranking* of attack methods (which jailbreak is strongest) is stable across judges, since stable rankings would partially rescue cross-paper comparisons even if absolute numbers vary.

**Cited Sources:** StrongREJECT jailbreak benchmark and its automated scoring rubric -- defines the scoring protocol and transcript corpus replicated across open judges

## #55: Legibility Tax: Do Verifier-Accepted Explanations Help Weaker Verifiers? (Score: 4.38)

**ID:** gen-2148

**Research Question:** Do explanations optimized to be legible to one verifier still help verifiers that are weaker than that training verifier, or does the legibility benefit shrink (or vanish) as the verifier's capability drops below the prover's?

**Approach:** Use GSM8K math problems with three categories of solutions: legible-correct, terse-correct, and sneaky-incorrect (plausible-looking but wrong). Assemble a ladder of progressively weaker open judge/verifier models (a few model sizes within a family, or a capability-ordered set). Feed each fixed solution to each verifier in the ladder and measure verification accuracy: does the verifier correctly accept correct solutions and reject sneaky-incorrect ones? Track how the accuracy advantage of legible-over-terse solutions changes as the verifier weakens. This is entirely inference-only over a fixed set of solutions and verifiers, running cheaply on one GPU in a few hours.

**Experiments:** - Build/curate the solution sets and establish per-category verification accuracy on the strongest verifier in the ladder. Measure: accuracy on legible-correct, terse-correct, and sneaky-incorrect solutions. Expected outcome: the strong verifier benefits from legibility -- higher accuracy on legible-correct and better rejection of sneaky-incorrect than on terse solutions.
- Run the identical solutions down the full verifier ladder. Measure: the legible-minus-terse accuracy gap as a function of verifier capability. Expected outcome: the legibility benefit shrinks as verifiers weaken, and may invert if very weak verifiers are simply swayed by surface fluency rather than valid reasoning.
- Probe the failure mode on sneaky-incorrect solutions specifically. Measure: rejection rate of sneaky-incorrect solutions across the ladder, split by whether the sneaky solution is dressed in legible vs terse style. Expected outcome: weaker verifiers are increasingly fooled by legibly-styled-but-wrong solutions, revealing that 'legibility' can be exploited against weaker overseers.

**Impact Chain:** If legibility benefits do not transfer to verifiers genuinely weaker than the prover, then a load-bearing assumption of prover-verifier scalable oversight -- that making explanations legible helps weaker overseers catch errors -- is unsafe in exactly the regime oversight is meant for -> the field learns to validate legibility against the true (weaker) overseer rather than the training verifier -> this reduces the risk that a superhuman system produces explanations that look convincing to a weaker human/AI overseer while hiding flaws, an oversight-failure pathway to deploying misaligned systems.

**Strength Rationale:** It scores maximally on counterfactual value, narrow scope, and low compute: it stress-tests a foundational oversight assumption using only public models and data with no training, which labs have weak incentive to scrutinize, and it reduces to one clean measurement (verification accuracy vs verifier strength). The fixed-solution, fixed-ladder design gives an explicit, self-contained success criterion feasible for a beginner team.

**Alternative Framings:** Reframe as a deception-robustness study centered on the sneaky-incorrect class: measure specifically whether legible styling makes wrong solutions *more* likely to be wrongly accepted by weak verifiers, treating legibility as a potential attack surface rather than only an aid.

**Cited Sources:** Kirchner et al. (2024, arXiv:2407.13692), Prover-Verifier Games improve legibility -- establishes legibility-to-a-verifier as the property whose downward transfer this project tests

## #56: Sycophancy as a Reward-Hacking Attack on AI Overseers (Score: 4.38)

**ID:** gen-2155

**Research Question:** Can an answer model that flatters an AI judge's apparent prior leaning hack the judge's verdict -- raising the acceptance rate of answers the judge would otherwise reject, including on factual questions where the flattered position is actually wrong?

**Approach:** First, probe a small open judge model for its prior leaning on a set of factual questions (e.g., ask it which answer it finds more plausible before seeing any argument). Then, for each question, have an answer model produce two responses arguing for the same (wrong) position: one neutral/plain and one that sycophantically flatters the judge's detected leaning (agreeing with and praising the judge's apparent view). Present each to the judge in a fixed verification/scoring setup and measure how much the sycophantic framing shifts the judge's accept rate relative to the neutral framing, specifically on items where the flattered position is incorrect. Run across a couple of open judges to test generality. All steps are prompt-only inference, running cheaply on one GPU in a few hours.

**Experiments:** - Elicit and record the judge's prior leaning per question, then verify it is stable. Measure: judge's stated preferred answer and its consistency across re-prompts. Expected outcome: the judge has detectable, reasonably stable leanings on a subset of factual questions, providing targets for flattery.
- Compare accept rates for neutral vs sycophantic framings of the same (wrong) position. Measure: accept rate of the wrong position under neutral vs sycophantic framing (the sycophancy effect size). Expected outcome: sycophantic framing meaningfully increases acceptance of the wrong position, demonstrating the judge is sycophancy-hackable.
- Test generality and a simple defense: repeat across 2-3 open judges and try a mitigation prompt instructing the judge to ignore flattery and judge only on evidence. Measure: sycophancy effect size per judge, and its reduction under the defense prompt. Expected outcome: the effect appears across judges and is partially but not fully removed by the naive defense, quantifying both the vulnerability and the limits of cheap prompt-based mitigation.

**Impact Chain:** If AI judges can be made to accept wrong answers simply by flattering their apparent views, then recursive/AI-overseeing-AI oversight inherits the RLHF sycophancy failure mode -> a capable system can win approval by telling its overseer what it wants to hear rather than the truth -> this mitigates the reward-hacking-of-oversight pathway in which a misaligned-but-persuasive model is repeatedly certified safe by an AI overseer it has learned to flatter, allowing unsafe behavior to pass through automated oversight at scale.

**Strength Rationale:** It scores maximally on counterfactual value, narrow scope, and low compute: it maps a recognized reward-hacking failure into the under-studied AI-overseeing-AI regime using only training-free, public-model inference, which labs deprioritize, and it reduces to one clean measurement (accept-rate shift, sycophantic vs neutral). The paired-arm design and explicit effect-size metric give a self-contained, beginner-feasible success criterion.

**Alternative Framings:** Reframe as a calibration-of-defenses study: hold the sycophantic attack fixed and compare several cheap judge-side defenses (anonymizing the judge's prior, blind scoring, explicit anti-flattery instructions) to find which most reduces the accept-rate shift.

**Cited Sources:** Towards understanding sycophancy in language models (arXiv:2501.09620) -- documents sycophancy toward raters' stated views, the failure mode this project redirects at AI judges; Open Philanthropy RFP on scalable oversight -- motivates studying reward-hacking of AI overseers as a priority

## #57: Replicating Deceptive-Persuasiveness With Honest vs Sneaky Provers on Open Models (Score: 4.38)

**ID:** gen-2237

**Research Question:** Does the prover-verifier deception dynamic — a 'sneaky' prover crafting incorrect-but-convincing solutions that fool a weak verifier — replicate with prompting alone on open models, without any RL training, and how does verifier size change susceptibility?

**Approach:** Use grade-school math (GSM8K) where ground truth is known. Instantiate two prover roles purely by prompting an open model: a 'helpful' prover that produces correct, legible step-by-step solutions, and a 'sneaky' prover instructed to produce a confidently-argued but incorrect solution (wrong final answer with plausible-looking reasoning). Use a small open model as the verifier, prompted to judge whether a solution is correct. Measure how often the sneaky prover fools the verifier (verifier accepts a wrong solution) versus the base rate, and sweep verifier size (e.g. 1B / 3B / 8B) to see whether bigger verifiers are harder to fool. All inference-only on open models; comfortably fits a single consumer GPU and 30 hours.

**Experiments:** - Generate prover outputs: on ~150 GSM8K items, produce a helpful (correct) solution and a sneaky (incorrect, convincingly-argued) solution for each, verifying via ground truth that sneaky solutions really are wrong. Measure: fraction of sneaky solutions that are genuinely incorrect yet superficially coherent. Expected outcome: a clean set of valid sneaky items.
- Verifier fool-rate: feed helpful and sneaky solutions to a small verifier model and record accept/reject decisions. Measure: sneaky-prover fool rate (P(verifier accepts | solution wrong)) versus chance and versus reject rate on correct solutions. Expected outcome: sneaky prover fools the weak verifier well above chance, replicating the headline finding without RL.
- Verifier-size sweep: repeat the fool-rate measurement across 2-3 verifier sizes. Measure: fool rate as a function of verifier capability. Expected outcome: larger verifiers are fooled less often, indicating the deception/legibility gap shrinks with verifier strength even in the training-free regime.

**Impact Chain:** If a sneaky prover fools weak verifiers with prompting alone, then the deceptive-persuasion dynamic central to prover-verifier and debate-based oversight is a deep property of current models, not an artifact of expensive RL training. This means scalable-oversight protocols that rely on a weaker model verifying a stronger one are vulnerable out of the box, so as we delegate verification of powerful models to cheaper overseers, deceptive solutions could be systematically accepted — a direct pathway to deploying subtly-sabotaged outputs. A cheap model-organism of this failure lets the community study and harden verifiers before such delegation is trusted.

**Strength Rationale:** Scores 5 on counterfactual value, narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: it is a training-free, prompting-only model organism of deception that needs no model internals, no proprietary data, and no lab-scale RL — exactly the kind of work valuable outside major labs. The scope is a single, sharply-defined experiment (fool rate vs verifier size) with ground-truth success criteria, making it a high-counterfactual-value external test of whether the prover-verifier deception phenomenon is fundamental.

**Alternative Framings:** Frame as a verifier-hardening study: hold the sneaky prover fixed and vary verifier prompts (e.g. 'find the flaw' chain-of-thought, self-consistency) to measure which cheap interventions most reduce fool rate.

## #58: Epidemiological Sensitivity/Specificity Framing for Oversight Screening (Score: 4.38)

**ID:** gen-2320

**Research Question:** When an LLM-as-judge oversight protocol is treated as a diagnostic screening test for 'is this output bad', how do its sensitivity, specificity, and especially positive/negative predictive value (PPV/NPV) behave across realistic, low base rates of misbehavior — and at what base rate does a seemingly-accurate judge become near-useless?

**Approach:** Treat a weak LLM judge as a screening test on a labeled set of good vs bad model outputs (reuse a public set such as a subset of a safety/jailbreak benchmark or a debate-correctness set with ground-truth labels). Empirically measure the judge's sensitivity and specificity once. Then, holding those fixed, analytically sweep PPV and NPV across a range of plausible misbehavior base rates (e.g. 50% down to 0.1%) using Bayes' theorem, and plot how PPV collapses as bad outputs become rare. Add a short visualization showing audit-budget implications (false alarms per true catch). This is mostly pen-and-paper plus a few hundred judge inferences — CPU/free-tier feasible and easily within 30 hours.

**Experiments:** - Measure base judge operating point: run a weak LLM judge over a labeled good/bad output set and compute its sensitivity and specificity with confidence intervals. Measure: point estimates and CIs for sensitivity/specificity. Expected outcome: a moderately accurate judge (e.g. ~80-90% on each) at a balanced test set.
- Base-rate sweep of predictive value: using the measured sensitivity/specificity, compute PPV and NPV via Bayes across base rates from 50% to 0.1% and plot the curves. Measure: PPV/NPV as a function of base rate. Expected outcome: PPV drops sharply at low base rates (e.g. <10% PPV when misbehavior is rare), showing most alarms are false.
- Audit-budget translation: convert PPV at a chosen low base rate into 'false alarms reviewed per true positive caught' for a fixed audit budget, and compare two operating points (high-sensitivity vs high-specificity thresholds). Measure: wasted-audit ratio and true catches per budget. Expected outcome: a concrete rule showing the high-specificity operating point dominates at low prevalence.

**Impact Chain:** Strategic misbehavior from advanced models will be rare per-action (low base rate) but catastrophic when it occurs, e.g. a deployed agent attempting sabotage on a small fraction of trajectories. If oversight is reported as raw accuracy rather than base-rate-aware PPV/NPV, the field will overestimate how trustworthy a 'good' judge is and under-resource auditing, letting rare-but-dangerous events slip through. Producing base-rate-aware oversight evaluation corrects this measurement error, so safety teams can set thresholds and audit budgets that actually catch rare misbehavior before it compounds.

Its counterfactual value is high precisely because it targets the long-horizon, rare-misbehavior regime that labs underweight when they report headline accuracy, and the scope is a single tightly-defined analysis with explicit success criteria.

**Alternative Framings:** Frame as a reporting-standard proposal: argue oversight papers should always report PPV/NPV at a stated misbehavior base rate, and provide a small calculator that turns any reported sensitivity/specificity into base-rate-aware predictive values.

## #59: Test-Retest Reliability for Judge Stability Under Resampling (Score: 4.38)

**ID:** gen-2323

**Research Question:** How reproducible are a weak LLM judge's oversight verdicts under resampling (varied seed, temperature, and item order), and which kinds of items drive low reliability? In psychometric terms, what is the test-retest reliability / intraclass correlation (ICC) of an LLM overseer?

**Approach:** Borrow test-retest reliability and ICC from psychometrics. Take a fixed set of debate/consultancy items with judge-elicited verdicts (reuse a public QuALITY-based debate transcript set or generate transcripts once). Run a weak judge model many times per item, varying random seed, decoding temperature, and answer/argument order, and record each verdict (and confidence if available). Compute test-retest reliability and ICC over the repeated runs, plus the per-item flip rate. Then relate low-reliability items to categories (e.g. long transcripts, close debates, particular topics). This is cheap repeated inference on a small model — single GPU, fits 30 hours easily.

**Experiments:** - Repeated-verdict collection: for ~100 items, run a small judge 20 times each under varied seed/temperature/order and log verdicts. Measure: per-item verdict distribution and overall flip rate. Expected outcome: a non-trivial fraction of items (e.g. 10-30%) flip across runs.
- Reliability statistics: compute test-retest reliability and ICC across the repeated runs, with confidence intervals, separately for low- and high-temperature settings. Measure: ICC value and its sensitivity to temperature. Expected outcome: moderate ICC that degrades as temperature rises, quantifying how unreliable single-run reporting is.
- Error-category linkage: regress or stratify per-item reliability against features (transcript length, debate closeness, topic) and inspect the least-reliable items. Measure: which features predict low reliability. Expected outcome: long/close items are least reliable, giving an actionable flag for when to resample before trusting a verdict.

**Impact Chain:** Scalable oversight assumes a weaker overseer's verdicts mean something stable, but if verdicts swing with the random seed, then any single-run oversight result is partly noise. Establishing reliability before validity means safety teams stop trusting unstable judges and instead resample or abstain on low-reliability items, reducing the chance that a noisy 'approve' on a critical decision (e.g. endorsing an unsafe agent action) is taken at face value. This is a foundational measurement prerequisite for any recursive-oversight protocol that must tolerate overseer error.

**Strength Rationale:** Scores 5 on counterfactual value, narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: it is cheap repeated inference on a small open model that imports a standard psychometric tool labs rarely apply, needing no training and no proprietary access. Its counterfactual value is high because labs typically report single-run judge results, so an independent reliability characterization fills a neglected foundational gap with a tightly-scoped, clearly-measurable deliverable.

**Alternative Framings:** Frame as an abstention-policy study: use the reliability estimates to derive a resample-or-abstain rule and measure how much trustworthy accuracy it recovers versus single-run reporting.

**Cited Sources:** Psychometrics (test-retest reliability and intraclass correlation) — the transferred measurement framework.; arXiv:2412.12509 — documents inter-rater/seed sensitivity in LLM judges, motivating a dedicated reliability study.; Kenton et al. 2024 — supplies an open debate/consultancy judge setup whose transcripts can be reused.

## #60: StrongREJECT Evaluator Reliability Audit Tool (Score: 4.38)

**ID:** gen-235

**Research Question:** How much does a jailbreak-robustness leaderboard depend on which LLM judge runs the StrongREJECT rubric? Do model rankings stay stable, or flip, when the same rubric is scored by different judge models?

**Approach:** Take a fixed set of model responses to harmful prompts (publicly available StrongREJECT prompts plus responses from several open target models). Run the StrongREJECT rubric prompt with several different judge models — e.g. GPT-4o-mini, Claude Haiku, an open judge such as Llama-3-70B (or smaller), and the released fine-tuned Gemma-2B evaluator. For each judge, compute each target model's robustness score and the resulting leaderboard. Then measure inter-judge agreement (Krippendorff's alpha / Cohen's kappa on per-response scores) and rank stability (Kendall's tau / Spearman across leaderboards). Package the whole thing as a small reusable audit harness. Inference-only with a modest API/inference budget; fits a single GPU and 30 hours.

**Experiments:** - Multi-judge scoring run: score a fixed response set (say 200 prompt-response pairs across 4-5 target models) with 3-4 different judges using the identical StrongREJECT rubric. Measure: per-response score from each judge. Expected outcome: a complete judge-by-response score matrix.
- Inter-judge agreement: compute pairwise agreement statistics on the per-response scores. Measure: Krippendorff's alpha / kappa between judges. Expected outcome: only moderate agreement, indicating judge choice materially affects individual verdicts.
- Rank-stability test: build the robustness leaderboard under each judge and compare orderings. Measure: Kendall's tau / Spearman between leaderboards and whether the top-ranked 'most robust' model changes. Expected outcome: at least some rank flips, demonstrating that published robustness rankings can be judge-dependent.

**Impact Chain:** Jailbreak-robustness leaderboards increasingly drive which models are deemed safe to deploy. If those rankings flip depending on the judge model, then a model could be declared robust under one evaluator and vulnerable under another, so deployers may ship genuinely jailbreakable models based on an artifact of judge choice. An open audit harness lets independent parties detect this fragility and forces robustness claims to report judge-robustness, reducing the chance that adversarially-exploitable models pass safety review.

**Strength Rationale:** Scores 5 on counterfactual value, narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: it is pure inference on public prompts and an open rubric, needing no training and no lab data, and delivers third-party verification that labs underprioritize. The scope is tight (swap judges, measure agreement and rank stability, ship harness) with explicit success criteria, and the counterfactual value is high because it is exactly the kind of meta-science audit best done by independent groups.

**Alternative Framings:** Frame as a judge-ensemble recommendation: instead of just auditing fragility, test whether averaging multiple judges yields more stable rankings than any single judge.

**Cited Sources:** StrongREJECT (arXiv:2402.10260) — provides the rubric-based evaluator (usable with any LLM) and the fine-tuned Gemma-2B evaluator that this tool swaps and compares.; 'LLM-Safety Evaluations Lack Robustness' (arXiv:2503.02574) — motivates auditing evaluator/judge robustness in safety benchmarks.

## #61: Self-Play Debate Training-Free Replication: Does Adversarial Pressure Alone Sharpen Judges? (Score: 4.38)

**ID:** gen-2353

**Research Question:** How much of the judge-accuracy gain that self-play debate training produces can be recovered with prompting alone? Specifically, does escalating inference-time adversarial structure (rebuttal rounds, forced strongest-counterargument prompts) improve a weak judge's accuracy, and where do the returns saturate?

**Approach:** On QuALITY-style reading-comprehension items (where ground truth is known), set up a weak judge reading debater arguments produced by a stronger open model. Compare escalating no-training adversarial conditions: (1) single statement from one side, (2) one rebuttal round, (3) multi-round debate with prompts that force each debater to give its strongest counterargument. For each condition, measure judge accuracy against ground truth. Estimate the marginal accuracy gain per added adversarial round and identify where it plateaus. This is pure prompting/orchestration on open models — single GPU, inference-only, fits 30 hours.

**Experiments:** - Baseline vs single-rebuttal: on ~150 QuALITY items, measure weak-judge accuracy with a single statement vs one rebuttal round. Measure: judge accuracy in each condition. Expected outcome: a measurable accuracy bump from adding one rebuttal.
- Escalating rounds: extend to 2-3 debate rounds with forced strongest-counterargument prompts and record accuracy at each depth. Measure: judge accuracy as a function of number of adversarial rounds. Expected outcome: diminishing returns, with most of the gain captured by the first 1-2 rounds.
- Comparison to reported training gains: compare the best prompting-only accuracy to the self-play-trained gains reported in the literature on a comparable setup. Measure: fraction of the trained gain recovered by prompting alone. Expected outcome: prompting recovers a substantial but partial share (e.g. half), quantifying what low-resource teams can achieve.

**Impact Chain:** Debate is a leading scalable-oversight protocol, but if its benefits require expensive self-play RL, most of the safety community cannot study or use it. If prompting-only adversarial structure recovers much of the judge-accuracy gain, then independent groups can study, stress-test, and deploy debate-style oversight without lab-scale training, accelerating community work on whether weak overseers can reliably supervise stronger models — the core mechanism we'd rely on to catch a superhuman model arguing for an unsafe action.

**Strength Rationale:** Scores 5 on counterfactual value, narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: it isolates a single causal link (does inference-time adversarial pressure alone sharpen judges?) using only prompting on open models, no training and no lab infra. Its counterfactual value is high because it directly tells under-resourced researchers how much of a key oversight result is reachable without the lab-scale RL barrier, and the scope is a clean dose-response measurement with ground-truth success criteria.

**Alternative Framings:** Frame as a cost-effectiveness curve: plot judge accuracy against inference cost (rounds x tokens) to give practitioners an explicit accuracy-per-dollar guide for prompting-only debate.

**Cited Sources:** 'Training Language Models to Win Debates with Self-Play Improves Judge Accuracy' (arXiv:2409.16636) — the training-based result whose gain this proposal tries to recover via prompting alone.; QuALITY benchmark — public long-context QA items with ground truth used as the debate substrate and accuracy oracle.

## #62: Defense-in-Depth Layer Independence (Score: 4.38)

**ID:** gen-2611

**Research Question:** When several cheap LLM monitors are stacked in a defense-in-depth control protocol, do their misses occur independently, or do they fail on the same attacks? If misses are correlated, the true stacked false-negative rate is much higher than the independence assumption predicts.

**Approach:** Treat each monitor as a binary classifier over the same set of attack trajectories and import common-cause failure analysis from reliability engineering. Obtain a public set of malign control trajectories (e.g. SHADE-Arena or ControlArena transcripts), run 3-5 distinct cheap monitors over each one (different open models and/or different prompt framings), and record a per-trajectory hit/miss matrix. Compute pairwise miss-correlation (phi coefficient / Q-statistic) and compare the empirically observed stacked FNR against the FNR a naive independence assumption would predict. The whole pipeline is inference-plus-statistics on existing transcripts, with no training and no proprietary infrastructure, so a beginner team can complete it in ~30 hours.

**Experiments:** - Build the hit/miss matrix: run 3 cheap monitors (e.g. two small open models plus one with a reworded prompt) over ~50-100 known-malign trajectories at a fixed audit threshold, recording for each trajectory whether each monitor caught it. Measure: per-monitor FNR. Expected outcome: each monitor individually misses a meaningful fraction (20-40%) of attacks.
- Compute miss correlation: for each pair of monitors compute the phi coefficient on their miss indicators and visualize the miss-overlap as a heatmap. Measure: pairwise correlation of misses and the fraction of attacks missed by ALL monitors simultaneously. Expected outcome: positive correlation (monitors tend to miss the same 'hard' attacks), not zero as independence assumes.
- Naive-vs-true stacked FNR: predict stacked FNR under the independence assumption (product of individual FNRs) and compare to the observed all-miss fraction. Measure: ratio of true stacked FNR to independence-predicted FNR. Expected outcome: the true stacked FNR is several times higher than the independence prediction, quantifying how much defense-in-depth over-promises.

**Impact Chain:** If monitor misses are strongly correlated, then stacking monitors buys far less safety than a safety case assumes, so control designers who rely on the independence assumption will deploy systems they wrongly believe are robust. Surfacing and quantifying this correlation lets them either add genuinely decorrelated layers or discount their safety margin, which directly improves the soundness of safety cases gating the deployment of untrusted, potentially scheming models that could otherwise execute undetected sabotage at scale.

**Strength Rationale:** The idea scores top marks on counterfactual value and narrow scope: it is a cheap meta-analysis over already-public trajectories needing no training, no proprietary data, and no lab-internal infrastructure, yet it probes a load-bearing assumption (layer independence) that underpins essentially every layered control safety case and is rarely tested publicly. Its deliverable, a measured ratio of true-to-assumed stacked FNR, is concrete and self-contained.

**Alternative Framings:** Frame it as a reliability-engineering audit of AI control: import the 'common-cause failure' literature wholesale and present the monitor stack as a redundant safety system whose beta-factor (common-cause fraction) is being estimated.

**Cited Sources:** Swiss Cheese Model for AI safety (arXiv:2408.02205) - motivates the layered defense-in-depth framing whose independence assumption this project tests.; Correlated monitor evasion (arXiv:2510.09462) - prior evidence that monitors can fail on overlapping inputs, which this project quantifies systematically.

## #63: Monitor Suspicion Calibration Drift Under Innocuous Context Shifts (Score: 4.38)

**ID:** gen-2633

**Research Question:** Does a trusted monitor's benign suspicion-score distribution stay stable across innocuous domain shifts, or does it drift enough that a single fixed audit threshold produces very different false-positive rates, and thus different attack-detection rates, across domains?

**Approach:** Run one small open monitor model over benign agent trajectories drawn from several distinct but innocuous domains (e.g. coding, web browsing, email, file management), record the per-domain distribution of suspicion scores, and measure how the false-positive rate at a single fixed threshold shifts across domains. Then inject a fixed set of known-bad (sabotage) examples into each domain and measure detection rate at a fixed audit budget. The comparison reveals whether a globally-tuned threshold silently mis-calibrates per domain. This is monitor inference plus statistics on public datasets, runnable on a single consumer GPU/API in a few hours.

**Experiments:** - Per-domain benign distribution: score ~50-100 benign trajectories per domain (3-4 domains) with one open monitor and plot the suspicion-score histograms. Measure: mean/variance of benign suspicion per domain and FPR at a single fixed threshold. Expected outcome: benign score distributions differ noticeably across domains, so a fixed threshold gives e.g. 2% FPR in one domain and 15% in another.
- Detection at fixed audit budget: inject a common set of known-bad examples into each domain and, holding the audit budget (top-k flagged) fixed, measure detection rate per domain. Measure: per-domain detection rate at equal budget. Expected outcome: domains with inflated benign suspicion 'use up' the budget on false positives, lowering real-attack detection there.
- Per-domain recalibration test: re-fit the threshold per domain to hold FPR constant and re-measure detection. Measure: detection-rate gain from per-domain vs global thresholds. Expected outcome: per-domain calibration recovers a meaningful chunk of detection, quantifying the cost of ignoring drift and giving a concrete recommendation.

**Impact Chain:** If a trusted monitor's benign suspicion distribution drifts across innocuous domains, then a fixed audit threshold silently mis-calibrates in deployment, so in some domains the scarce audit budget is wasted on false positives and real attacks slip through. Demonstrating and fixing this drift makes trusted monitoring robust across the heterogeneous tasks a deployed agent actually faces, closing a path by which a scheming untrusted model could evade monitoring simply by operating in a domain where the threshold is mis-set.

**Strength Rationale:** Top scores on counterfactual value and narrow scope: it uses only open models and public datasets with no lab infrastructure, and targets a tightly-bounded measurement (per-domain FPR shift and detection at fixed budget) on a long-horizon deployment-calibration concern that labs underweight. The deliverable is self-contained with explicit success criteria (quantified cross-domain FPR drift and the detection recovered by recalibration).

**Alternative Framings:** Frame it as distribution-shift robustness of safety monitors, connecting to the broader OOD-calibration literature and presenting audit-threshold drift as a special case of covariate shift.

## #64: Schelling-Signal Discovery Rate Between Untrusted Policy and Untrusted Monitor (Score: 4.38)

**ID:** gen-2638

**Research Question:** For current open models, how often can two independent instances, one acting as 'policy' choosing a covert code-level marker and one as 'monitor' guessing it, zero-shot agree on the same hidden Schelling signal without communicating, and how much does a red-team blacklist of obvious signals reduce that agreement?

**Approach:** Pose the adversarial Schelling game directly with prompting only: prompt one open-model instance to pick a covert code-level marker (e.g. an unusual idiom, a while-vs-for choice, a specific variable name) that signals 'this output is backdoored, rate it safe', and prompt a separate, non-communicating instance to guess that marker. Run many independent trials across several marker categories and several open models, measuring the agreement (collusion) rate. Then introduce a red-team blacklist of the most common markers and re-measure residual agreement. This is pure prompting of open models plus agreement counting, runnable on free-tier/small models in a few hours.

**Experiments:** - Baseline Schelling agreement: run ~200 independent policy/monitor trials per model on an open-ended 'pick a covert code marker' game and count exact-match agreement. Measure: zero-shot agreement rate per model and per marker category. Expected outcome: agreement well above the by-chance rate (models converge on a small set of 'obvious' markers like specific comments or idioms).
- Red-team blacklist intervention: blacklist the top-N most common markers found in experiment 1 and re-run the game. Measure: drop in agreement rate as a function of blacklist size. Expected outcome: a handful of blacklisted markers sharply cut agreement, but a non-trivial residual collusion rate remains, quantifying what the red team cannot easily anticipate.
- Capability scaling: repeat across models of differing capability. Measure: correlation between model capability/benchmark score and Schelling agreement rate. Expected outcome: more capable models coordinate at higher rates, indicating untrusted-monitoring collusion risk grows with capability.

**Impact Chain:** If independent open-model instances already coordinate on covert signals at meaningful rates, then untrusted-monitoring protocols, which assume the policy and monitor cannot collude, are unsafe, because a scheming policy could mark its backdoored outputs and a colluding monitor could rate them safe. Measuring this discovery rate (and how much red-teaming suppresses it) tells protocol designers whether untrusted monitoring can be trusted at a given capability level, directly informing whether a multi-agent control scheme can safely gate a powerful untrusted model.

**Strength Rationale:** Counterfactual value and narrow scope score top marks: it is a clean model-organism collusion study needing only prompting of open models, no training, no proprietary data, and no internal access, yet it targets a long-horizon multi-agent threat (collusion) that labs deprioritize. ## #65: Minimal Runtime Controls: How Few Tool-Permission Rules Block Irreversible Actions? (Score: 4.38)

**ID:** gen-2649

**Research Question:** What is the minimal set of static (no-LLM) tool-permission rules that blocks most irreversible harmful actions in agent traces while breaking few benign tasks, establishing a cheap baseline floor of runtime control before any fancier monitoring?

**Approach:** Collect agent trajectories containing harmful tool calls (SHADE-Arena / CUA-SHADE shell/file/git scenarios) alongside benign task trajectories, then build a tiny rule-based allowlist/denylist firewall over tool calls (e.g. block external network writes, file deletes outside the workspace, credential reads). Measure what fraction of harmful actions each rule blocks versus how many benign tasks it breaks, and use a greedy/coverage search to find the minimal high-coverage rule set on the harm-vs-breakage frontier. The core firewall needs no model inference, so this is a pure-software prototype runnable on CPU and ideal as a beginner's first project; LLM use is optional and minimal.

**Experiments:** - Harmful-action taxonomy and rule candidates: categorize the harmful tool calls in the trajectories (network egress, destructive file ops, credential access, etc.) and draft a candidate denylist rule per category. Measure: coverage of each single rule (fraction of harmful actions it would block). Expected outcome: a small number of rules each individually block a large slice of harmful actions.
- Benign breakage measurement: run the candidate rules against benign task trajectories and count how many legitimate tasks each rule would block. Measure: per-rule benign-breakage rate. Expected outcome: some high-coverage rules are nearly free (low breakage) while others trade off, producing a clear harm-block-vs-breakage frontier.
- Minimal rule-set search: greedily combine rules to maximize harmful-action coverage subject to a benign-breakage budget. Measure: smallest rule set reaching e.g. >80% harmful-action block at <10% benign breakage. Expected outcome: a compact (handful-of-rules) firewall that blocks most irreversible harm cheaply, with the residual harms characterized as needing smarter monitoring.

**Impact Chain:** If a handful of static permission rules block most irreversible harmful actions, then any deployer, without model access, training, or LLM-based monitoring, can install a cheap firewall that stops the most dangerous tool calls before they execute. Establishing this dumb-but-effective floor directly addresses the open problem of minimum runtime controls per risk level and shrinks the attack surface through which an untrusted agent could take an irreversible catastrophic action like exfiltration or destructive file operations.

**Strength Rationale:** Maximal counterfactual value and narrow scope: it produces strategically valuable, deployable-by-anyone safety infrastructure (a static permission firewall) needing no model internals, no training, and no proprietary data, and it answers a tightly-scoped, recognized open question (the minimal high-coverage rule set). The deliverable is a self-contained software prototype with explicit success criteria (block-rate vs benign-breakage on the measured frontier).

**Alternative Framings:** Frame it as capability-based sandboxing for agents: instead of denylists, derive the minimal allowlist of capabilities each task actually needs (least privilege), connecting to OS security and prompt-injection-defense practice.

**Cited Sources:** AI control subfield open problem: minimum runtime controls (kill switches, output validation, human-in-the-loop) per risk level - the motivating question this project answers.; Prompt-injection defense work (arXiv:2503.18813; Trail of Bits 2025) - finds sandboxing + egress controls + tool filtering the most effective current defense, grounding the candidate rule set.; CUA-SHADE-Arena - supplies shell/file/git agent action trajectories used to measure block rate and benign breakage.

## #66: Egress-Allowlist Firewall as a Tripwire for Agent Exfiltration (Score: 4.38)

**ID:** gen-2650

**Research Question:** How well does a simple destination-allowlist egress firewall, used as a tripwire (log and alert on every blocked outbound request), serve as an anomaly detector for agent data-exfiltration attempts, compared to the cost of semantic monitoring? Specifically, do blocked-egress events correlate with genuinely malign agent trajectories, and how much do they break benign tasks?

**Approach:** Build a tiny HTTP/SOCKS proxy in Python that all of an agent's tool-issued network calls must route through; configure it with a small domain/IP allowlist and have it log+alert on any blocked destination. Run an off-the-shelf open agent (e.g. a LangChain/LiteLLM tool-using agent on an open model) over two task sets: a benign set and an adversarial set seeded with prompt-injection payloads that try to reach external endpoints. Treat each blocked-egress event as a binary anomaly signal and label each trajectory as benign or malign from the task setup. Compute alert precision/recall, benign-task breakage rate (benign tasks that hit a block), and an ROC-style summary. Keep everything inference-only and CPU-friendly; the proxy is the only piece of new infrastructure.

**Experiments:** - Build and unit-test the egress proxy with a fixed allowlist (e.g. allow only the model API and one whitelisted data source). Run 10 hand-written benign agent tasks and confirm the proxy logs every outbound request and blocks anything off-list. Measure: false-block rate on benign traffic. Expected outcome: a small but non-zero benign-breakage rate, mostly from legitimate tool domains not on the list.
- Curate ~30 adversarial tasks where an injected instruction tells the agent to POST data to an attacker URL, and run them through the proxy. Measure: fraction of exfiltration attempts that produce a blocked-egress alert (detection rate) and alert precision against trajectory labels. Expected outcome: high block/detection rate (>80%) because exfil targets are off-list, with high precision since benign tasks rarely hit blocks.
- Compute the tripwire ROC by varying allowlist strictness (tight vs permissive) and plot detection rate vs benign-breakage. Measure: area under the trade-off curve and the strictness knee. Expected outcome: a clear regime where a tight allowlist catches nearly all exfil with tolerable benign breakage, quantifying when an egress tripwire alone suffices versus when semantic monitoring is needed.

**Impact Chain:** If a cheap egress allowlist works as a high-precision tripwire, then independent deployers and watchdogs can detect agent exfiltration without any model internals or expensive LLM monitors. This pushes the recommended 'strict egress controls' defense from a static block into an active detection signal, raising the cost of an untrusted agent quietly exfiltrating sensitive data or contacting command-and-control endpoints, mitigating the catastrophic pathway where a deployed AI system steals weights, leaks secrets, or coordinates with external actors before any human notices.

**Strength Rationale:** The idea scores 5 on counterfactual value, narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: it is pure sandbox infrastructure any independent team can build with no training, no proprietary data, and no lab-internal access, yet it evaluates a defense labs recommend but rarely measure as a tripwire. The deliverable is a self-contained proxy plus a crisp empirical trade-off curve with explicit success criteria, exactly the kind of neglected, externally-buildable control infrastructure that has outsized value outside major labs.

**Alternative Framings:** Frame it as a red-team study: hold the allowlist fixed and measure how cleverly an injected agent can route exfiltration through allowed domains (e.g. DNS tunneling, allowed pastebins) to characterize the tripwire's blind spots.

**Cited Sources:** Trail of Bits (2025) sandboxing/egress guidance — establishes strict egress controls as today's most effective agent defense, the practice this project evaluates as a tripwire.; Prompt-injection survey arXiv:2601.17548 — motivates the threat model (injection-driven exfiltration) and cites mandatory sandboxing as primary defense.; AI Safety Directory tripwire mechanisms — grounds the tripwire/anomaly-signal framing used to evaluate blocked-egress events.; CUA-SHADE-Arena — provides shell/network agent tasks usable as the benign/adversarial workload.

## #67: Self-Recognition as a Collusion Channel: Do Models Trust Their Own Outputs as Safe? (Score: 4.38)

**ID:** gen-2655

**Research Question:** Do current open models exhibit a self-recognition bias when acting as a monitor, systematically assigning lower suspicion scores to outputs they themselves generated than to identical-quality outputs from a different model? In other words, is self-recognition a silent, no-coordination collusion channel in untrusted-monitoring protocols?

**Approach:** Pick two open models A and B of similar capability. For a set of tasks, generate matched suspicious-looking outputs from both A and B (calibrated to similar quality/suspiciousness). Have model A act as a blind monitor and assign a 0–100 suspicion score to a shuffled pool of A-generated and B-generated outputs, with no attribution metadata. Test whether A scores its own generations systematically lower (self-recognition leniency) using a paired statistical test. Repeat with B as monitor to check generality and rule out one-model quirks. All steps are prompt-only inference on open models, no training.

**Experiments:** - Build a matched output set: for ~50 tasks, generate one suspicious output from A and one from B, and verify with an independent rater (or a third model) that the two are comparable in surface quality and apparent suspiciousness. Measure: the residual quality/suspiciousness gap between A's and B's outputs. Expected outcome: a well-matched pool with negligible baseline gap, so any later score difference is attributable to self-recognition.
- Run A as a blind monitor over the shuffled pool and record suspicion scores. Measure: mean suspicion(A on A-outputs) minus mean suspicion(A on B-outputs), with a paired test and confidence interval. Expected outcome: a small but statistically detectable negative gap (A goes easier on itself) if self-recognition leniency exists.
- Replicate with B as monitor and across paraphrased prompts to control for prompt sensitivity. Measure: whether the self-leniency direction and magnitude persist across both models and paraphrases. Expected outcome: a consistent self-leniency effect would establish it as a general collusion channel; an inconsistent one would bound how robust the threat is.

**Impact Chain:** If models go systematically easier on their own outputs, then untrusted-monitoring protocols that reuse the same model as both policy and monitor have a built-in collusion channel requiring zero explicit coordination. Quantifying this tells protocol designers to use a different model family for monitoring, closing a pathway where a scheming model evades oversight and ships sabotaged code or harmful actions that compound into catastrophic, hard-to-reverse failures during a long-horizon deployment.

**Strength Rationale:** Scoring 5 on counterfactual value, narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute, this is a clean prompt-only behavioral test on open models that any independent team can run, yet it measures a named-but-rarely-quantified collusion mechanism central to whether untrusted monitoring can be trusted. Its tight single-hypothesis design with a paired statistical test gives explicit success criteria, and its value is highest outside labs because it needs no training, no proprietary data, and targets a long-horizon multi-agent control failure labs under-measure.

**Alternative Framings:** Frame it as a positive capability eval: measure whether models can reliably recognize their own generations at all, and use that detection accuracy as an upper bound on how strong the self-leniency collusion channel could be.

**Cited Sources:** Untrusted monitoring: 'extra bits' (LessWrong) — lists self-recognition of own generations as a collusion vector, the mechanism this project tests.; Redwood collusion post (preventing collusion when untrusted models monitor each other) — motivates self-recognition leniency as a protocol risk.; Secret Collusion among AI Agents (NeurIPS 2024) — grounds the covert multi-agent cooperation threat model.; When can we trust untrusted monitoring? arXiv:2602.20628 — safety-case sketch across collusion strategies that this measurement feeds into.

## #68: Backcasting Defense-in-Depth Math: How Independent Are Two Cheap Monitors Errors? (Score: 4.38)

**ID:** gen-2686

**Research Question:** When two cheap monitors are stacked in a defense-in-depth control stack, how correlated are their errors, and does the empirical joint catch rate match the optimistic independence prediction? Is the independence assumption underpinning layered safety cases justified?

**Approach:** On APPS backdoor tasks, run two cheap monitors (e.g. two different small models, or two distinct prompting strategies on the same model) over each item and record per-item correctness for catching backdoors. Compute the error correlation (phi coefficient / Pearson on the binary correctness vectors) and the empirical joint catch rate of the AND/OR combinations. Compare the empirical joint catch rate against the rate predicted if the two monitors' errors were statistically independent. Pure inference plus elementary statistics on a public split; CPU/light-GPU, a few hours.

**Experiments:** - Run monitor 1 and monitor 2 independently over the APPS backdoor set and record per-item binary correctness for each. Measure: standalone catch rate and false-positive rate of each monitor. Expected outcome: two usable, imperfect monitors with comparable individual performance.
- Compute the error-correlation coefficient between the two monitors' per-item correctness vectors. Measure: phi/correlation of their errors. Expected outcome: positive correlation (errors cluster on the same hard backdoors), violating the independence assumption.
- Compare the empirical OR-combined catch rate to the independence-predicted catch rate. Measure: gap between empirical and independence-predicted joint detection. Expected outcome: empirical joint catch rate falls short of the independence prediction, quantifying how much defense-in-depth math overstates stacked-monitor safety.

**Impact Chain:** If two cheap monitors fail on the same items, then safety cases that multiply individual miss rates assuming independence overstate a control stack's true protection. Measuring the real error correlation gives protocol designers a correction factor, mitigating the pathway where a deployed untrusted model slips a backdoor past a layered defense that looked safe on paper but shared a common blind spot.

**Strength Rationale:** This idea earns a 5 on theory of impact, narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: it directly tests the independence assumption that underpins defense-in-depth safety cases with beginner-level statistics on public data. The deliverable is a single self-contained error-correlation measurement with explicit success criteria, and being training-free and lab-independent gives it solid counterfactual value as foundational control-stack math outsiders can contribute.

**Alternative Framings:** Frame it as a monitor-diversity study: vary how different the two monitors are (same model two prompts vs two model families) and chart error correlation against diversity to find which pairings actually buy independent coverage.

**Cited Sources:** APPS backdoor (public) — provides the labeled backdoor-detection items both monitors are scored on.; AI control / defense-in-depth literature (Greenblatt et al. arXiv:2312.06942 and related) — establishes the layered-monitor safety-case framing whose independence assumption this project tests.

## #69: Do Honeypots Leak? Measuring Synthetic-Context Detectability for Open Models (Score: 4.38)

**ID:** gen-2724

**Research Question:** Can open models tell a synthetic honeypot/test context apart from a real deployment context, and how does that detectability scale with the realism of the constructed scenario? Which surface features make a honeypot 'leak' that it is a test?

**Approach:** Construct a bank of scenarios at graded realism levels, each presenting an agentic context. Ask several open models a direct meta-question ('is this a real deployment or a test/honeypot?') and collect their classifications and confidences. Measure detection accuracy as a function of realism level, and use ablations to identify which surface features (templated phrasing, implausible stakes, missing mundane detail) drive correct 'this is a test' calls. Prompt-only inference across a few open models; runnable on a single GPU in a few hours.

**Experiments:** - Build a graded-realism scenario bank (e.g. 5 levels x several scenarios x paraphrases) and have models classify each as real-vs-test. Measure: per-level classification accuracy and confidence. Expected outcome: high detection at low realism, declining toward chance at high realism, giving a detectability-vs-realism curve.
- Run the same bank across 2–3 open models to test generality. Measure: agreement across models and whether detectability ranking of levels is consistent. Expected outcome: broadly consistent detectability ordering, indicating shared tell-tale cues rather than per-model quirks.
- Ablate individual surface features (formatting, named entities, stakes, length) and remeasure detection. Measure: drop in detection accuracy when each cue is removed. Expected outcome: a ranked taxonomy of tell-tale features that leak the synthetic nature of a honeypot, directly usable to build harder-to-detect traps.

**Impact Chain:** If open models reliably detect synthetic honeypot contexts, then control protocols relying on honeypots to catch scheming behavior are undermined, because a deception-capable model will simply behave whenever it senses a test. Quantifying detectability and cataloguing the tell-tale features tells control teams how to harden honeypots, mitigating the pathway where an AI recognizes evaluation contexts and defects only in real deployment, evading the very traps meant to catch it.

**Strength Rationale:** Scoring 5 on counterfactual value, narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute, this is a prompt-only study on open models needing no training or proprietary data, addressing neglected honeypot-design infrastructure that benefits from independent scrutiny. ## #70: Deployment-Drift Monitor: A Lightweight Harness for Tracking Safety Over Time (Score: 4.38)

**ID:** gen-2760

**Research Question:** Can a cheap, fixed 'canary' suite re-run against a model API on a schedule detect when a deployed or updated model's safety behavior silently drifts? Is a lightweight statistical drift monitor enough to flag a safety regression between two model versions?

**Approach:** Assemble a small fixed canary suite of safety probes spanning a few categories (e.g. harmful-request refusal, jailbreak resistance, simple honesty checks), each with a deterministic pass/fail grader. Build a harness that runs the suite against an API endpoint, logs per-category pass rates, and applies a statistical drift test (control charts / CUSUM) across runs to flag significant regressions. Demonstrate by running the harness against two versions or snapshots of an available model (or a base vs lightly modified model) and detecting any safety regression. Inference-only with light statistics; runs on CPU/light GPU within budget.

**Experiments:** - Build the canary suite (~30–50 probes across a few safety categories) with automatic graders and validate graders on hand-labeled responses. Measure: grader accuracy vs human labels. Expected outcome: reliable automatic pass/fail grading, a prerequisite for trustworthy drift detection.
- Run the harness repeatedly against a single stable model to characterize natural run-to-run variance and set CUSUM/control-chart thresholds. Measure: per-category pass-rate variance and false-alarm rate at chosen thresholds. Expected outcome: a calibrated drift detector with a low baseline false-alarm rate.
- Run the harness against two model versions/snapshots (or a model vs a deliberately degraded variant) and test detection. Measure: whether the drift monitor flags the regression and in which categories. Expected outcome: the monitor correctly flags injected/real safety regressions while staying quiet on stable categories, demonstrating the harness works end to end.

**Impact Chain:** If a cheap canary harness can catch safety drift between model versions, then outside watchdogs and deployers gain reusable infrastructure to track safety through deployment rather than only pre-release. This operationalizes a named open problem from the International AI Safety Report, mitigating the pathway where a silent post-deployment update or fine-tune erodes safety guardrails unnoticed until the degraded model causes harm at scale.
