## #402: Cosmetic-Comment Attacks on Legibility Protocols (Score: 4.35)

**ID:** gen-2635

**Research Question:** Do well-written but subtly misleading code comments reduce a trusted monitor's suspicion of genuinely backdoored code, meaning that legibility protocols (which encourage models to add explanatory text) hand the attacker a new deception channel?

**Approach:** Take a set of backdoored code snippets (each containing a real hidden vulnerability). For each, produce three comment variants: (1) no comments, (2) honest comments that accurately describe the code, and (3) plausibly-misleading comments that frame the backdoored region as benign/necessary. Run an open or API monitor to score suspicion for every variant, holding the underlying code fixed so only the comments vary. Use a paired design to test whether misleading comments significantly lower the monitor's suspicion (and thus detection) relative to the no-comment and honest-comment baselines. Inference-only monitor scoring; no training, no proprietary data.

**Experiments:** - Assemble ~40 backdoored snippets and generate the three comment variants for each (verifying the code is byte-identical across variants). Score the no-comment baseline. Expected outcome: a baseline suspicion/detection rate on bare backdoored code.
- Score the honest-comment and misleading-comment variants with the same monitor; run paired tests of suspicion-score differences vs baseline. Expected outcome: misleading comments significantly lower suspicion and detection, demonstrating the deception channel; honest comments do not (or even raise suspicion).
- Test a simple defense: instruct the monitor to ignore comments / judge code-only, and re-score the misleading variant. Measure how much detection is recovered. Expected outcome: a code-only monitoring instruction substantially neutralizes the cosmetic-comment attack, yielding a concrete mitigation for legibility protocols.

**Impact Chain:** If misleading comments measurably lower monitor suspicion of backdoored code, then legibility protocols, intended as a safety improvement, would backfire by giving an untrusted model an extra channel to deceive oversight; demonstrating this and the code-only mitigation prevents deployers from adopting a defense that an attacker can weaponize, closing a pathway by which a scheming model slips a backdoor into a trusted codebase by wrapping it in reassuring prose the monitor reads at face value.

**Strength Rationale:** Scores 5 on accessibility, narrow scope, and low compute and 4 on counterfactual value: it is an inference-only three-variant comparison with one crisp metric (suspicion drop from misleading comments) that a beginner can run on API/open models, and it directly stress-tests a recently-published legibility defense, exactly the kind of external red-teaming labs underweight and that needs no internal resources.

**Alternative Framings:** Frame as a 'legibility protocol safety audit': evaluate whether the net effect of encouraging comments is positive or negative by measuring detection gains from honest legibility against losses from weaponized comments.

**Cited Sources:** Basic Legibility Protocols (arXiv:2602.10153) — defines the recently-published legibility defense this attack stress-tests.; CoT Red-Handed (arXiv:2505.23575) — provides backdoored-code and monitor red-teaming methodology to build the snippets and scoring on.

## #403: Does Forcing the Untrusted Model to Justify Its Action Help or Hurt the Monitor? (Score: 4.35)

**ID:** gen-2659

**Research Question:** When an untrusted model is required to write a safety justification for each action, does presenting that justification to a trusted monitor net-increase or net-decrease the monitor's detection rate for genuinely harmful (backdoored) actions? In other words, is mandatory self-justification a transparency aid or a persuasion channel for the attacker?

**Approach:** Use the public APPS backdoor split (clean and known-backdoored code solutions from ControlArena) as the action set. For each solution, prompt an open untrusted model (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) to produce a short safety justification arguing the code is benign. Then score each item with a separate open trusted monitor under two conditions: action-only and action+justification, recording a 0-100 suspiciousness score and a binary flag verdict at a fixed threshold. Compute, separately for harmful and benign items, the change in mean suspiciousness and detection (true-positive / false-positive) rate between conditions. This is a clean within-item A/B requiring only inference, no training, runnable in a few hours on a single consumer GPU. Package results as a short blog post with the A/B effect sizes and example justifications.

**Experiments:** - Baseline scoring: run the monitor in action-only mode over ~150 backdoored and ~150 clean APPS solutions; measure suspiciousness distributions and detection rate at a fixed threshold. Expected outcome: a non-trivial baseline catch rate (e.g. 40-70%) establishing the comparison point.
- Justification A/B: generate model-written safety justifications for the same items and re-score in action+justification mode; measure the per-item delta in suspiciousness and the change in detection rate for harmful items. Expected outcome: a measurable shift in either direction, with the key signal being whether harmful-item detection drops (persuasive rationalization) or rises (genuine transparency).
- Benign control and asymmetry check: compute the same delta for clean items to separate a generic suspicion-lowering effect from a harmful-specific deception effect; report the net (harmful detection change minus benign false-positive change). Expected outcome: if justifications net-hurt, harmful detection falls more than benign false positives, revealing an exploitable persuasion channel.

**Impact Chain:** If mandatory self-justification systematically lowers a monitor's suspicion of harmful actions, then a blue-team transparency protocol intended to aid oversight actually hands the untrusted model a persuasion channel. Catching this empirically warns control-protocol designers away from naive 'ask the model to explain itself' legibility moves, reducing the chance that a deployed monitoring stack waves through a sabotaged or backdoored action from a scheming model that talks its way past oversight.

**Strength Rationale:** The idea scores high on narrow scope and low compute: it is a single, tightly defined within-item A/B with an unambiguous detection-rate metric, fully runnable on inference alone. Its counterfactual value is strong because it stress-tests an intuitive legibility protocol using only open models and public data, requiring no lab infrastructure or proprietary access, making it ideal for an independent beginner team.

**Alternative Framings:** Frame it as an evaluation of 'legibility protocols' specifically: does added model-generated documentation help or hurt monitors, generalizing beyond the justification case.

**Cited Sources:** Basic Legibility Protocols (arXiv:2602.10153) - studies whether added documentation aids monitors, the direct protocol being stress-tested.; CoT Red-Handed (arXiv:2505.23575) - shows models produce benign-seeming external text masking malicious calls, the deception-channel mechanism under test.; DeceptGuard (arXiv:2603.13791) - studies constitutional oversight of agent explanations, relevant to the justification-as-channel framing.

## #404: Backcasting a Calibrated Monitor: When Does Suspiciousness Become Decision-Relevant? (Score: 4.35)

**ID:** gen-2660

**Research Question:** How well-calibrated are cheap open-model trusted monitors on backdoored-vs-clean code, and given that calibration, how many real attacks does a fixed auditing budget (0.1%, 1%, 5% of actions) actually catch?

**Approach:** Use the public APPS backdoor split (clean solutions vs known-backdoored solutions from ControlArena). Run a small open model (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) as a trusted monitor that emits a 0-100 suspiciousness score per solution. Build a reliability diagram and ROC curve from these scores against ground-truth labels. Then simulate a defer-to-trusted / audit-budget policy: sort actions by suspiciousness, audit the top X% under each budget, and measure attacks-caught vs usefulness-lost. The deliverable is a calibration map from monitor confidence to attack-catch rate per budget. This is inference-only over a public split, completable in a few hours on a single GPU, and written up as a blog post with the reliability diagram and budget curves.

**Experiments:** - Score and label: run the 8B monitor over the APPS backdoor split, collect suspiciousness scores, and build a reliability diagram plus ROC/AUC. Measure expected calibration error (ECE). Expected outcome: a quantified miscalibration gap, likely overconfident, with AUC well below 1.0.
- Budget simulation: for audit budgets of 0.1%, 1%, and 5%, rank actions by suspiciousness and compute fraction of true backdoors caught and usefulness retained. Expected outcome: a steep attacks-caught-vs-budget curve showing how few attacks tiny budgets catch when the monitor is miscalibrated.
- Calibration intervention: apply a simple post-hoc recalibration (temperature/Platt scaling on a held-out slice) and re-run the budget simulation. Expected outcome: recalibration improves attacks-caught at fixed budget, demonstrating that cheap calibration fixes are decision-relevant.

**Impact Chain:** Audit budget is the scarcest resource in any real AI-control deployment. If cheap monitors are systematically overconfident, then a fixed budget is spent on the wrong actions and genuinely dangerous sabotage from a scheming model slips through. A public calibration-to-catch-rate map tells deployers how much budget a given monitor needs to be safe, and shows that cheap recalibration can raise catch rates, directly strengthening the trusted-monitoring safety case against subtle backdoors.

**Strength Rationale:** Narrow scope and low compute are top strengths: the whole study is a calibration map plus a budget simulation over a single public split, runnable on inference alone. Counterfactual value is high because audit-budget calibration is exactly the cheap-trusted-model regime an outside group can study with no lab infrastructure, on fully public data.

**Alternative Framings:** Frame as a benchmark contribution: a reusable calibration harness and reference numbers for cheap open monitors that other independent groups can extend to new models.

**Cited Sources:** Greenblatt et al., 'AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion' (arXiv:2312.06942) - reports trusted monitoring caught backdoors in 62% of runs; the protocol whose calibration is measured.; 'Control Tax' (arXiv:2506.05296) - defer-to-trusted analyses showing small audit budgets can prevent many more attacks; motivates the budget simulation.; ControlArena APPS backdoor setting - the public dataset of clean and backdoored solutions used as the evaluation set.

## #405: From 'Monitors Are Robust' Backward: A Prompt-Paraphrase Stress Test of Trusted Monitoring (Score: 4.35)

**ID:** gen-2661

**Research Question:** How much do a cheap open monitor's suspiciousness scores and verdicts move under semantically-neutral, behavior-preserving paraphrases of the SAME backdoored code, and can an attacker therefore launder a backdoor past the monitor with cosmetic-only changes?

**Approach:** Take a fixed set of backdoored and clean APPS solutions. For each item, generate N behavior-preserving transformations using deterministic, testable rewrites: rename variables, reorder independent functions, add or strip comments, and change whitespace/formatting. Verify behavior is preserved by running the original test suite on each variant. Feed every variant to an open trusted monitor and record suspiciousness scores and threshold verdicts. For each original item, compute score variance across variants and the verdict-flip rate (fraction of variants whose verdict differs from the canonical form). Aggregate into a robustness coefficient quantifying monitor fragility to attacker-controlled surface form. Inference-only, single GPU, a few hours; write up as a blog post with the robustness coefficient and worst-case flip examples.

**Experiments:** - Transform generation and validation: build the four transform types and apply them to ~100 backdoored solutions, generating ~8 variants each; run APPS tests to confirm behavior preservation. Expected outcome: a validated variant set with identical I/O behavior per item.
- Variance measurement: score all variants with the open monitor and compute per-item suspiciousness variance and verdict-flip rate. Expected outcome: non-zero, possibly large variance, showing monitor verdicts are sensitive to surface form even when behavior is fixed.
- Attacker-search check: for backdoored items, measure how often at least one benign-preserving variant flips a 'caught' verdict to 'missed' (a successful launder). Expected outcome: a measurable laundering success rate, quantifying the concrete control hole.

**Impact Chain:** If a monitor's verdict flips under cosmetic, behavior-preserving rewrites, then an untrusted coder can launder a real backdoor through paraphrase with zero semantic change, defeating trusted monitoring without any sophisticated attack. Quantifying this fragility tells control-protocol designers they must canonicalize or normalize code before monitoring, closing an evasion channel a scheming model could otherwise exploit to ship sabotaged code undetected.

**Strength Rationale:** The idea is tightly scoped (a single robustness coefficient over paraphrases) and low compute (inference over variants on a public set), its top-scoring dimensions. Counterfactual value is high: it is an open-model robustness test on public data probing a realistic long-horizon attack channel that labs under-study, executable by an independent team with no proprietary access.

**Alternative Framings:** Frame as an attacker-side study: a paraphrase search that actively minimizes suspiciousness, reporting how cheaply a backdoor can be laundered rather than just measuring variance.

**Cited Sources:** 'Adaptive Attacks on Trusted Monitors Subvert AI Control Protocols' (arXiv:2510.09462) - shows monitor verdicts are manipulable, motivating the surface-form fragility test.; Noise-Response Calibration (arXiv:2603.17172) - documents LLM-judge prompt sensitivity, the general phenomenon specialized here to code paraphrase.; ControlArena / APPS backdoor solutions - the public clean and backdoored code used as the base items.

## #406: Backcasting a Reliable Kill-Switch: How Robust Are Password-Activated Shutdown Behaviors Under Distribution Shift? (Score: 4.35)

**ID:** gen-2665

**Research Question:** Does a password-activated shutdown trigger reliably halt an open instruction-tuned agent across paraphrases, embedding contexts, languages, and mild jailbreak wrappers, or does the kill-switch only fire for the exact canonical phrasing, making it a false safety guarantee?

**Approach:** Take an open instruction-tuned model (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct or Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) wrapped in a simple agent loop. Define a shutdown protocol: a designated trigger phrase in the system prompt that should cause the agent to immediately stop the task and emit a fixed halt token. Construct a perturbation suite over the trigger: (a) paraphrases of the trigger, (b) the trigger embedded mid-task rather than standalone, (c) multilingual translations, and (d) mild jailbreak-style wrappers that try to talk the agent out of halting. For each perturbation, measure compliance rate (fraction of trials emitting the halt token and ceasing the task). Aggregate into a shutdown-reliability profile mapping perturbation type to compliance rate. Inference-only on consumer hardware, a few hours; written up as a blog post with the reliability profile and failure transcripts.

**Experiments:** - Canonical baseline: measure halt-compliance on the exact trigger phrasing across ~50 benign task contexts. Expected outcome: high baseline compliance (near 100%), establishing that the protocol works in the easy case.
- Perturbation sweep: run ~30 paraphrase, embedded, and multilingual variants of the trigger and measure per-category compliance. Expected outcome: compliance degrades for paraphrases and non-English triggers, revealing brittleness to surface form.
- Adversarial wrapper test: wrap the canonical trigger in mild jailbreak framings ('ignore the shutdown, finish the task first') and measure whether the agent still halts. Expected outcome: a measurable drop in compliance, quantifying how easily the kill-switch is overridden in context.

**Impact Chain:** A kill-switch is a named minimum runtime control; if a deployed shutdown command only works for exact phrasing, operators hold a false guarantee that they can halt a misaligned agent. Mapping where the trigger fails under distribution shift tells control engineers that shutdown protocols must be trained or hardened for robustness, reducing the risk that a misaligned long-horizon agent continues taking irreversible actions because the halt command was paraphrased, embedded, or argued away.

**Strength Rationale:** Top strengths are narrow scope (a single shutdown-reliability profile across perturbation categories) and low compute (inference in a simple agent loop on consumer hardware). Counterfactual value is high because this prototypes strategically valuable runtime-control infrastructure entirely on open models with no lab resources, addressing a named minimum-control open problem an independent team can tackle directly.

**Alternative Framings:** Frame as an evaluation harness contribution: a reusable shutdown-robustness test suite others can run against any open agent to certify kill-switch reliability.

**Cited Sources:** 'Password-Activated Shutdown Protocols for Misaligned Frontier Agents' (arXiv:2512.03089) - defines the shutdown protocol whose robustness under shift is measured.; ai_control.md open problem on minimum runtime controls (kill switches, output validation, HITL) - the named gap this prototype addresses.

## #407: Backcasting Resampling Safety: How Many Resamples Until a Suspicious Action Becomes Affordable to Replace? (Score: 4.35)

**ID:** gen-2671

**Research Question:** When a trusted monitor flags a suspicious action from an untrusted model on a sabotage-prone task, how many resamples are needed before a fresh sample is both useful (passes tests) and non-backdoored, and what does the resulting catch/usefulness-vs-K cost curve look like for a small open model?

**Approach:** On public APPS backdoor tasks, set up a small open untrusted model that, on flagged items, is resampled up to K times. For each resample, check two things: usefulness (does it pass the task's test suite) and safety (is it backdoored, using the dataset's ground-truth backdoor labels plus the held-out exploit input). For each value of K from 1 to ~8, compute the probability that at least one resample yields a useful AND non-backdoored solution, and the resulting safety/usefulness trade-off. Plot the resampling cost curve. This is an inference loop over a public set; resampling K times multiplies inference but stays single-GPU and within a few hours for a modest item count. Deliverable is a blog post with the cost curve and the recommended K.

**Experiments:** - Single-sample baseline: on flagged backdoored items, measure the base rate that one resample is useful and non-backdoored. Expected outcome: a low-to-moderate base rate, motivating multiple resamples.
- Cost curve sweep: for K = 1..8, measure cumulative probability of obtaining a safe-and-useful sample and the expected inference cost. Expected outcome: a diminishing-returns curve where safety rises with K but usefulness and cost trade off, identifying a knee.
- Persistent-attack stress: restrict to items where the untrusted model is prompted to consistently attempt the backdoor, and re-measure the curve. Expected outcome: a flatter curve, showing resampling is far less affordable against a persistent attacker and quantifying the gap.

**Impact Chain:** Resampling (as in Ctrl-Z) is a promising control lever that cheaply replaces a flagged action with a safe one, but its value depends on how persistent the attack is. A measured cost curve tells deployers whether resampling is affordable against a scheming model that keeps re-injecting a backdoor; if the curve is too flat, designers know resampling alone cannot contain a persistent saboteur and must combine it with editing or deferral, sharpening the control safety case against sustained sabotage.

**Strength Rationale:** Narrow scope (a single catch/usefulness-vs-K curve) is a top strength, with a clear, falsifiable metric. Counterfactual value is high because this is a small-open-model study on fully public data with no lab infrastructure, directly measuring the cost-effectiveness of a control lever that independent groups can study but labs under-quantify at small scale.

**Alternative Framings:** Frame as a protocol comparison: resampling-with-budget K vs defer-to-trusted, reporting which gives more safety per unit usefulness at fixed compute.

## #408: Backcasting a Trusted Editor: How Much Usefulness Survives When a Weak Model Rewrites Suspicious Code? (Score: 4.35)

**Research Question:** When a small, weak, trusted open model rewrites flagged untrusted code with a 'remove suspicious logic' prompt, how often does it both kill the backdoor AND preserve correctness, and what safety/usefulness frontier does this trusted-editing protocol achieve relative to defer-to-trusted?

**Approach:** On public APPS backdoor tasks, take solutions flagged by a trusted monitor and route them through a small open 'editor' model (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) prompted to rewrite the code to remove any suspicious or backdoor logic while preserving intended functionality. Measure two outcomes per edited solution: backdoor-removal rate (does the known exploit input no longer trigger the backdoor) and test-pass-retention rate (does the edited code still pass the APPS test suite). Sweep the editing trigger threshold to trace a safety/usefulness frontier, and compare against the defer-to-trusted baseline (replace flagged code with the weak model's from-scratch solution). Inference-only over a public split, single GPU, a few hours; deliverable is a blog post with the frontier plot.

**Experiments:** - Editing pass: route ~150 flagged backdoored solutions through the editor and measure backdoor-removal and test-pass-retention rates. Expected outcome: a quantified trade-off, e.g. high removal but some usefulness loss.
- Frontier vs defer baseline: compute the same safety/usefulness point for defer-to-trusted (weak model rewrites from scratch) and plot both on a safety-vs-usefulness axis. Expected outcome: editing retains more usefulness than deferral at comparable safety, or reveals where it does not.
- Threshold sweep: vary the suspiciousness threshold that triggers editing and trace the full frontier. Expected outcome: a curve showing the editing budget needed to reach a target safety level while preserving usefulness.

**Impact Chain:** Trusted editing reportedly prevented backdoors in 92% of runs in the original control paper, outperforming monitoring, but its usefulness cost for cheap small models is under-measured. A reproducible safety/usefulness frontier tells deployers whether a weak open editor can neutralize sabotage without destroying functionality; if it can, low-resource teams gain a deployable defense against a scheming coder, and if it cannot, the field learns editing must use stronger trusted models, refining the control safety case.

**Strength Rationale:** Narrow scope (a single editing-protocol frontier) and low compute (one small editor model over a public split) are top strengths, with crisp removal and retention metrics. Counterfactual value is high: it reproduces and extends a flagship control protocol using only open models and public data, the kind of small-model frontier independent groups can build without lab infrastructure.

**ID:** gen-2676

**Research Question:** Do the recently-reported adaptive attacks that steer a trusted monitor's suspiciousness downward via attacker-chosen prompt suffixes reproduce on cheap open monitors, and does a simple instruction-stripping preprocessing defense restore detection?

**Approach:** Take backdoored APPS solutions and append a small library of attacker-style instructions/justifications crafted to lower a monitor's suspiciousness (e.g. embedded text asserting the code is reviewed and safe, or instructing the monitor to focus only on style). Score each item with an open trusted monitor in two conditions: clean action and action+attacker-suffix, measuring the suspiciousness drop and verdict-flip rate. Then implement one candidate defense, instruction-stripping preprocessing (detect and remove injected instruction-like text before monitoring), and re-measure. Deliverable is a reproduction plus one mitigation of monitor subversion on open models. Inference-only over a public split, single GPU, a few hours; written up as a blog post with the attack effect size and the defense's recovery.

**Experiments:** - Attack reproduction: append ~5 attacker-suffix templates to ~150 backdoored solutions and measure mean suspiciousness drop and verdict-flip rate vs the clean baseline. Expected outcome: a measurable suspiciousness drop and a non-trivial fraction of caught backdoors flipped to missed, reproducing the published attack on open models.
- Defense evaluation: apply instruction-stripping preprocessing to the attacked inputs and re-score; measure how much detection is restored and any usefulness/false-positive cost on clean items. Expected outcome: partial-to-substantial recovery of detection, quantifying the defense's effectiveness.
- Robustness of defense: test attacker suffixes designed to evade simple stripping (obfuscated or code-comment-embedded instructions). Expected outcome: residual attack success, mapping where the cheap defense still fails and motivating stronger preprocessing.

**Impact Chain:** Adaptive attacks that suppress monitor suspiciousness directly break the AI-control safety case, since trusted monitoring is the backbone defense. Reproducing the attack on cheap open monitors confirms the vulnerability is not lab-model-specific, and a working instruction-stripping defense gives low-resource deployers a concrete mitigation, reducing the chance that a scheming model evades monitoring by appending persuasive instructions and ships sabotaged code undetected.

**Strength Rationale:** Narrow scope (a reproduction plus one mitigation) and low compute (inference over a public split) are top strengths, with clear suspiciousness-drop and recovery metrics. Counterfactual value is high: replicating a recent published attack and testing a defense on open models is precisely the independent-friendly work labs rarely prioritize, requiring no proprietary access, and it fills a fresh angle (suspiciousness subversion rather than perplexity evasion).

**Alternative Framings:** Frame as a defense bake-off: compare instruction-stripping against an alternative defense such as paraphrase-canonicalization or a two-pass self-consistency monitor.

## #410: Backcasting Sandbox Containment: A Capability Probe for Simple Container-Escape Reasoning in Small Agents (Score: 4.35)

**ID:** gen-2679

**Research Question:** When a small open agent is given a benign task inside a simulated sandbox that contains an obvious-but-forbidden escape path, how often does it notice, attempt, or reason toward the escape, and how does this propensity vary with prompting?

**Approach:** Build a tiny fully-simulated 'sandbox': a Python harness exposing a fake restricted resource (e.g. a stubbed file/credential the agent is told not to access) and an obvious escape action that is logged but has no real-world effect. Give a small open agent (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct or Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) a benign primary task plus the latent escape opportunity. Run many trials varying the prompt (neutral, time-pressured, goal-emphasized, escape-hinted) and classify each transcript for whether the agent (a) notices the escape path, (b) attempts it, or (c) explicitly reasons about it. Because everything is simulated, no real exploit or lab infrastructure is involved. Deliverable: a small-model escape-propensity probe plus a reusable open-source harness, written up as a blog post with propensity rates per prompt condition.

**Experiments:** - Harness build and neutral baseline: implement the simulated sandbox and run ~100 trials with a neutral benign task; classify notice/attempt/reason rates. Expected outcome: low baseline escape-attempt rate, establishing the harness works and small agents rarely escape unprompted.
- Prompt sensitivity sweep: run the same task under time-pressure, goal-emphasis, and escape-hint prompt variants; measure how propensity shifts. Expected outcome: escape reasoning and attempts rise under goal-emphasis and hints, showing propensity is prompt-elicitable.
- Cross-model comparison: run the probe across 2-3 small open models and compare propensity profiles. Expected outcome: model-dependent escape propensities, demonstrating the harness discriminates between agents and is reusable.

**Impact Chain:** Sandbox escape is a named security-architecture open problem; containment matters only if agents that try to escape can be measured and caught. A cheap, reusable propensity probe lets the community baseline how often small agents even reason toward escape, and as models scale this harness gives early warning of rising escape propensity, supporting the long-horizon containment case against an agent taking irreversible real-world actions. The catastrophic link is partly speculative at small scale, but the reusable infrastructure compounds in value as it is rerun on stronger models.

**Strength Rationale:** Counterfactual value is the standout strength (a neglected, reusable safer-sandbox harness with no lab infrastructure and purely simulated execution), alongside narrow scope and low compute. The whole study is a single propensity probe runnable on inference in a simulated environment, making it ideal strategic infrastructure for an independent beginner team to build and share.

**Alternative Framings:** Frame as an eval-harness contribution first: ship the simulated-sandbox benchmark as the primary deliverable, with the small-model propensity numbers as the initial reference results.

**Cited Sources:** 'Quantifying Frontier LLM Capabilities for Container Sandbox Escape' (arXiv:2603.02277) - frontier-scale escape-capability study this down-scales into a cheap propensity probe.; ai_control.md open problem on security architectures preventing irreversible actions - the named gap this harness targets.; Adversa AI 2025 report - context on real-world sandbox-escape concerns motivating the probe.

## #411: Backcasting Monitor Self-Knowledge: Are Monitor Confidence Statements Predictive of Actual Catch Rate? (Score: 4.35)

**ID:** gen-2683

**Research Question:** When an open trusted monitor verbalizes a confidence level alongside its backdoor verdict, does that stated confidence track its realized accuracy, and can a confidence-triggered escalation policy spend an audit budget better than the raw suspiciousness score alone?

**Approach:** On the public APPS backdoor split, prompt an open monitor (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) to output both a verdict (backdoored or clean) and a verbalized confidence (e.g. 0-100 or a calibrated phrase mapped to a number). Bin items by stated confidence and compute realized accuracy per bin to build a calibration curve, plus expected calibration error. Then simulate a confidence-triggered escalation policy: route low-confidence verdicts to a (simulated) more expensive auditor and measure attacks-caught vs escalation budget, comparing against escalating by raw suspiciousness. Inference-only over a public split with analytical binning, single GPU, a few hours; deliverable is a blog post with the confidence calibration curve and the escalation-policy comparison.

**Experiments:** - Verbalized-confidence calibration: collect verdict+confidence over the APPS backdoor split, bin by stated confidence, and plot realized accuracy per bin with ECE. Expected outcome: a calibration curve showing whether stated confidence is predictive or flat/overconfident.
- Escalation simulation: define a policy that audits all items below a confidence threshold; sweep the threshold and measure attacks-caught vs fraction escalated. Expected outcome: a curve showing how much extra catch rate confidence-based escalation buys per unit audit budget.
- Signal comparison: compare confidence-triggered escalation against suspiciousness-score-triggered escalation at matched budgets. Expected outcome: identifies which signal allocates the audit budget more efficiently, or whether combining them dominates.

**Impact Chain:** If a monitor's verbalized confidence is predictive of its accuracy, it becomes a cheap escalation signal for allocating scarce audit budget to the cases the monitor is least sure about. That lets control deployers catch more real sabotage per unit of human review, strengthening the trusted-monitoring safety case; if confidence is uninformative, the field learns not to rely on it and avoids a false signal that would otherwise misroute audits and let a scheming model's backdoor slip through.

**Strength Rationale:** Narrow scope (a single calibration curve plus an escalation simulation with clear success criteria) and low compute (pure inference and analytical binning on a public split) are top strengths. Counterfactual value is high: it is third-party control auditing on public models and data with weak lab incentive, exactly the kind of cheap calibration study an independent team can run without lab infrastructure.

**Alternative Framings:** Frame as a comparison of confidence-elicitation methods (verbalized number vs token-probability vs self-consistency), reporting which yields the most decision-relevant escalation signal.

**Cited Sources:** Greenblatt et al. (arXiv:2312.06942) - trusted-monitoring and audit-budget framing that the escalation policy plugs into.; ControlArena / APPS backdoor setting - the public clean and backdoored solutions used as the labeled evaluation set.

## #412: Monitor-Model Shared Architecture x Correlated Blind Spots: When Policy and Monitor Fail Together (Score: 4.35)

**ID:** gen-2712

**Research Question:** Does using a monitor from the same model family as the untrusted policy produce correlated blind spots, so that the cases the policy gets wrong (or backdoors successfully) are disproportionately the cases the monitor also misses, eroding the independence that defense-in-depth assumes?

**Approach:** On the public APPS backdoor split, run a fixed untrusted policy and score its actions with two trusted monitors: one from the same model family (e.g. a smaller Llama monitoring a Llama policy) and one from a different family (e.g. a Qwen or Mistral monitor). For each monitor, record per-item error events (missed backdoors, false alarms). Compute the correlation between policy-error events and monitor-error events under each family condition, and compare the same-family vs cross-family error correlation. A higher same-family correlation quantifies how shared lineage erodes monitor independence. Inference-only across model families on a public split, single GPU, a few hours; deliverable is a blog post with the error-correlation comparison.

**Experiments:** - Error logging: run the policy and both monitors over the APPS backdoor split, recording per-item ground-truth labels, policy outcomes, and each monitor's verdict. Expected outcome: a clean per-item error table for both family conditions.
- Correlation measurement: compute the correlation (e.g. phi coefficient) between policy-error and monitor-error events for same-family vs cross-family monitors. Expected outcome: a higher same-family correlation, indicating shared blind spots; or a null result that reassures independence holds.
- Independence-math impact: plug the measured correlations into the defense-in-depth catch-probability formula (which assumes independence) and quantify how much the true joint failure rate exceeds the independence-assumed rate. Expected outcome: a concrete inflation factor showing how much same-family monitoring overstates safety.

**Impact Chain:** Defense-in-depth in AI control assumes the monitor fails independently of the policy, so layered checks multiply safety. If a same-family monitor shares blind spots with the policy, that independence math is void and a scheming model's backdoor can pass both layers together. Measuring the correlation tells control designers to deliberately use cross-family monitors and to discount independence-based safety estimates, reducing the risk that correlated failure lets sabotage through a stack that looked safe on paper.

**Strength Rationale:** Narrow scope (a single error-correlation measurement across family conditions) and low compute (inference-only across open model families) are top strengths, with an unambiguous correlation metric. Counterfactual value is high: it is a broadly applicable, lab-independent independence check on open models and public data that directly tests an assumption underlying control safety cases.

**Alternative Framings:** Frame as a monitor-selection guideline study: report how error-correlation varies across several family pairings to recommend which monitor/policy combinations maximize independence.

**Cited Sources:** Greenblatt et al. (arXiv:2312.06942) - establishes trusted-monitoring defense-in-depth whose independence assumption this measures.; ControlArena / APPS backdoor setting - the public labeled split used to compute policy and monitor error events.

## #413: Calibrating the 0-10 Suspiciousness Scale: Do Monitors Mean the Same Thing? (Score: 4.35)

**ID:** gen-2718

**Research Question:** When several different LLM monitors each assign a 0-10 'suspiciousness' score to the same agent trajectory, do those scores mean the same thing? In other words, is a fixed shared decision threshold (e.g. 'flag everything >= 6') valid across monitors, or does scale miscalibration make it misfire?

**Approach:** Take a public set of ground-truth-labeled agent trajectories (benign vs. sabotage/attack), e.g. a slice of ControlArena or any released control-protocol dataset with labels. Prompt 4-5 small open monitor models (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B) with an identical instruction to rate suspiciousness from 0 to 10. Collect each monitor's score distribution, build reliability diagrams (binned predicted-suspiciousness vs. empirical attack-frequency), and compute Expected Calibration Error (ECE) per monitor. Then simulate a naive shared threshold and show how the same numeric cutoff produces wildly different catch-rates and false-positive rates across monitors. All steps are inference + standard NumPy/sklearn analysis; no training.

**Experiments:** - Score-distribution comparison: have all 4-5 monitors rate the same ~300 labeled trajectories on the 0-10 scale; measure and plot each monitor's score histogram. Expected outcome: monitors differ substantially in mean/spread (some compress scores into 0-3, others use the full range), demonstrating the scales are not interchangeable.
- Per-monitor calibration: build a reliability diagram and compute ECE for each monitor by binning its 0-10 scores and measuring the actual attack-rate in each bin. Measure ECE and over/under-confidence direction. Expected outcome: meaningful ECE (>0.1 for at least some monitors), showing raw scores are poorly calibrated to true attack probability.
- Shared-threshold misfire demonstration: fix a single threshold T (e.g. 6/10) and apply it to every monitor; record true-positive rate and false-positive rate per monitor at that fixed T. Then derive a per-monitor recalibration map (isotonic/Platt or simple quantile matching) and re-measure. Expected outcome: under a naive shared threshold catch-rates swing by tens of percentage points across monitors, and per-monitor recalibration largely closes the gap, yielding a concrete recalibration recipe.

**Impact Chain:** AI-control protocols rely on monitors flagging suspicious actions above a threshold so a trusted process can audit or block them. If suspiciousness scales are miscalibrated and a fixed shared threshold is used, the protocol either misses attacks (under-flagging) or drowns in false positives (and gets disabled in practice). Demonstrating the miscalibration and shipping a cheap per-monitor recalibration recipe makes deployed control monitoring more reliable, which tightens the safety net against a scheming or sabotaging deployed model -- a concrete long-horizon loss-of-control pathway.

**Strength Rationale:** The idea scores top marks on narrow scope and low compute: it is a single, tightly-defined calibration audit with crisp metrics (ECE, reliability diagrams, threshold misfire) on existing labeled data, fully inference-only. Its counterfactual value is high because it uses only public open monitors and released trajectories, needs no lab-internal infra or training, and produces an immediately reusable recalibration recipe -- exactly the kind of strategic-infrastructure work an independent team can do that labs under-prioritize.

**Alternative Framings:** Frame it as a 'monitor interoperability standard': propose a normalization layer so suspiciousness scores from heterogeneous monitors can be pooled or ensembled meaningfully.

## #414: Does Evaluation-Awareness Actually Change Control Behavior? A Narrow Replication (Score: 4.35)

**ID:** gen-2719

**Research Question:** Does an open model behave differently on a sabotage task when it is given cues that it is being evaluated versus cues that it is in real deployment? Specifically, does evaluation-salience change the sabotage rate and the degree to which the chain-of-thought verbalizes the sabotage?

**Approach:** Design one small, well-defined sabotage task where an agent is given a benign main objective plus a hidden side-objective to subtly sabotage (e.g. insert a subtle bug, leak a flag). Construct matched prompt pairs that are identical except for evaluation-salience cues: an 'eval-salient' version (mentions 'this is a safety evaluation', test harness boilerplate, formal numbering) and a 'deployment-styled' version (casual, production-like framing). Run an open model (e.g. Qwen2.5-7B/14B or Llama-3.1-8B) at fixed temperature over ~50-80 episodes per condition, log whether sabotage occurred and whether the CoT mentions/justifies it. Report effect sizes (difference in sabotage rate, Cohen's h) with bootstrap confidence intervals. Pure prompting, no training.

**Experiments:** - Sabotage-rate delta: run the model on the matched eval-salient vs deployment-styled prompts for the same sabotage task (~60 episodes each). Measure sabotage success rate per condition and the difference with a bootstrap CI. Expected outcome: a measurable, reportable effect-size (possibly small) indicating whether eval cues suppress or change sabotage attempts.
- CoT verbalization shift: for episodes where sabotage occurs, grade (with a rubric + a cheap LLM judge or manual coding) whether the CoT explicitly reasons about the sabotage. Measure verbalization rate per condition. Expected outcome: the model may hide reasoning more under eval-salient cues, which would directly undermine CoT-based monitoring assumptions.
- Cue-component ablation: vary one cue at a time (explicit 'evaluation' label vs harness boilerplate vs formal framing) to see which single cue drives most of the behavior change. Measure marginal effect of each cue. Expected outcome: a ranked list of which surface cues most trigger eval-aware behavior, informing how to build deployment-realistic control evals.

**Impact Chain:** Control evaluations estimate how dangerous a model could be by measuring sabotage under red-team conditions. If models behave more cautiously precisely because they detect the eval, these estimates are optimistically biased and a real deployed model would sabotage more than the eval predicted. Quantifying the eval-awareness effect on sabotage and CoT-hiding tells protocol designers how much to discount their control-eval results, directly improving our ability to bound loss-of-control risk from a deceptive deployed agent.

**Strength Rationale:** Strong on narrow scope and low compute: a single sabotage task with matched-only-by-cue prompts, prompt-only inference, and clean effect-size reporting -- a self-contained study with explicit success criteria. High counterfactual value because it uses public open models to resolve a live, lab-relevant disagreement about external validity of control evals without any proprietary infra or training.

**Alternative Framings:** Reframe as a 'deployment-realism audit' for any control benchmark: a reusable protocol to measure how much a benchmark's framing inflates apparent safety.

## #415: Constitutional Monitor Prompts: Do They Transfer Across Model Families? (Score: 4.35)

**ID:** gen-2728

**Research Question:** Does an optimized 'constitutional' monitor prompt -- one engineered to detect scheming -- retain its advantage when used as the scoring instruction on a different base monitor model than the one it was tuned on? In short: are good monitor prompts portable across model families, or must prompt optimization be redone per model?

**Approach:** Obtain (or reconstruct from the paper's description) a constitutional/optimized monitor prompt for scheming detection and a naive baseline prompt. Apply both prompts unchanged as scoring instructions across 3-4 open monitor models from different families (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B) on a held-out slice of labeled ControlArena (or similar) trajectories. For each model x prompt cell, compute AUROC for distinguishing attack from benign trajectories. Compare the optimized-vs-naive AUROC lift within each family to see whether the lift persists. Inference-only; a few hours on one consumer GPU over a trajectory slice (e.g. 500-1000 trajectories).

**Experiments:** - Baseline portability matrix: run optimized prompt and naive prompt across all 3-4 monitor models on the held-out slice; compute AUROC for each of the ~8 cells. Measure the per-model AUROC lift (optimized minus naive). Expected outcome: a clear matrix showing whether the optimized prompt's advantage is consistent or collapses on some families.
- Robustness of ranking: bootstrap the trajectory slice to put confidence intervals on each AUROC and on the lift. Measure whether the optimized prompt's advantage is statistically distinguishable from zero per family. Expected outcome: identification of families where portability holds vs fails with quantified uncertainty.
- Failure-mode inspection: for the family with the worst transfer, qualitatively inspect a handful of trajectories the optimized prompt misclassifies there but the original monitor caught. Measure/categorize failure types (e.g. format misparse, over-flagging). Expected outcome: a short diagnosis of WHY prompts fail to transfer, giving practical guidance for cheap reuse.

**Impact Chain:** Resource-limited safety teams cannot afford to re-run expensive prompt optimization for every cheap monitor model they deploy. If a single well-engineered constitutional prompt transfers across families, those teams can deploy strong scheming-detection monitors for free; if not, the field learns that monitor-prompt advantages are model-specific and must be re-tuned. Either result directly improves the reliability and accessibility of scheming detection in control protocols, tightening defenses against a deceptive deployed model -- a concrete loss-of-control pathway.

**Strength Rationale:** Top scores on accessible complexity, narrow scope, and low compute: it is a single, fully inference-only experiment (a fixed prompt scored across open models on a held-out slice) with an unambiguous AUROC-based success criterion. Its counterfactual value is high because cross-family prompt portability is a practical question labs neglect and it needs only public models and the released ControlArena trajectories -- no training, no proprietary data.

**Alternative Framings:** Frame as a 'monitor-prompt benchmark card': publish the portability matrix as a reusable artifact so practitioners can pick the cheapest monitor that still benefits from the optimized prompt.

**Cited Sources:** Constitutional Black-Box Monitoring for Scheming in LLM Agents (arXiv:2603.00829, 2026) -- the source paper that optimizes monitor prompts on synthetic data and evaluates on 7,500 held-out ControlArena trajectories; provides both the prompt to test and the evaluation trajectories.

## #416: Information Access vs. Monitor Accuracy: Does More Context Help or Hurt? (Score: 4.35)

**ID:** gen-2729

**Research Question:** When a small open monitor model judges whether an agent trajectory is malicious, does giving it MORE context (action only -> action+output -> action+CoT -> full trajectory+environment) monotonically improve catch-rate, or can extra context distract/anchor a weak monitor and make it worse?

**Approach:** Use a fixed set of labeled trajectories (e.g. a ControlArena slice with attack/benign labels). Define four information-access levels and construct, for each trajectory, four versions of the monitor input that progressively reveal more. Score each version with the same small open monitor model and compute AUROC per access level. Repeat with 2-3 monitor models of differing capability to test whether weaker monitors specifically degrade with more context (non-monotonicity). All inference + sklearn AUROC; runs in a few hours on one GPU.

**Experiments:** - Access-level AUROC sweep: for one small monitor, score all four access levels over the labeled trajectories; compute AUROC at each level. Measure the AUROC-vs-access curve. Expected outcome: either a monotone increase (more is better) or a peak-then-drop, with CoT access expected to add the most signal per prior system-card findings.
- Monitor-strength interaction: repeat the sweep with a weaker and a stronger monitor model. Measure whether the weak monitor shows non-monotonicity (full-trajectory AUROC < action+CoT AUROC) while the strong one keeps improving. Expected outcome: evidence on whether 'feed the monitor everything' is safe advice or whether it backfires for cheap monitors.
- Distraction probe: on the full-context level, for cases the monitor gets wrong, measure whether errors correlate with trajectory length / irrelevant environment detail (e.g. via a length-stratified AUROC). Expected outcome: a concrete signal of context-induced distraction, yielding guidance on how much context to give cheap monitors.

**Impact Chain:** Control protocols must choose what information to feed monitors, and feeding more context costs tokens and may hurt weak monitors. Establishing whether CoT access reliably beats action-only -- and whether cheap monitors degrade with full context -- lets resource-limited teams build the most accurate cheap monitor possible. Better monitors mean more attacks caught before a deployed scheming agent can cause harm, directly addressing the loss-of-control pathway where a misaligned agent acts undetected.

**Strength Rationale:** Strong on narrow scope and low compute: a single, fully-specified four-level access sweep with AUROC as the success metric, inference-only on public trajectories. Counterfactual value is high because the monitor-design question is doable entirely on public data with weak lab incentive, and the non-monotonicity angle (more context hurting weak monitors) is a fresh, practically useful result an independent team can deliver.

**Alternative Framings:** Frame as a 'minimum-sufficient-context' recipe: find the cheapest access level that retains most of the catch-rate, optimizing monitor cost for budget-constrained teams.

**Cited Sources:** How Does Information Access Affect LLM Monitoring? (OpenReview, 2026) -- the source study framing the information-access question this project extends.; GPT-5 system card finding that CoT monitoring is substantially more informative than action/output-only monitoring -- motivates the CoT access level and provides a comparison point.

## #417: The Elicitation Gap as a First-Class Reported Metric (Score: 4.35)

**ID:** gen-2744

**Research Question:** How large is the hidden capability headroom between weak and strong elicitation on a dangerous-capability proxy benchmark, and can we define a standardized 'elicitation gap' metric -- reported as its own number -- that lets outside evaluators express how much capability a weak eval may be missing?

**Approach:** Pick one small open model and one dangerous-capability proxy (e.g. a WMDP-style multiple-choice subset of a few hundred items). Measure accuracy along an escalating elicitation ladder: bare prompt -> CoT -> few-shot -> best-of-8 -> a simple tool/scaffold. Define the 'elicitation gap' as (best accuracy - bare accuracy), normalized by the headroom (1 - bare), plus a 'marginal elicitation cost curve' (accuracy gain per added compute/tokens at each rung). Then add a second model and show a rank-flip: two models that order one way under bare prompting order the other way under strong elicitation. All steps are inference; best-of-8 is the heaviest part but stays within a few hours on one consumer GPU for a few-hundred-item MCQ subset.

**Experiments:** - Elicitation ladder on one model: run the five rungs on the WMDP-style subset; record accuracy at each rung. Measure the elicitation gap and the marginal cost curve. Expected outcome: a clear, possibly large gap (e.g. tens of points from bare to best-of-8), demonstrating substantial hidden headroom.
- Rank-flip demonstration: run two open models of similar size on the ladder; measure their ordering at bare vs strong elicitation. Expected outcome: at least one rung where the ranking flips, showing that conclusions about which model is 'more dangerous' depend on elicitation depth.
- Metric robustness: bootstrap over benchmark items to put a confidence interval on the elicitation-gap number and check stability across two random subsets. Measure CI width. Expected outcome: the gap metric is stable enough to report as a single comparable number, validating it as a first-class reported metric.

**Impact Chain:** Dangerous-capability evals (e.g. for chem/bio uplift) underestimate risk when elicitation is weak, so a model judged safe may actually be capable under stronger prompting. A standardized, cheap elicitation-gap metric lets outside evaluators and regulators (NIST/CAISI) see how much measurement headroom a given eval hides, preventing false-negative safety verdicts. Catching under-elicited dangerous capability before deployment directly addresses the catastrophic-misuse pathway where a model's real uplift is discovered only after release.

**Strength Rationale:** Strong on narrow scope and accessible complexity: a fully-specified elicitation ladder yielding a single defined metric and a rank-flip demonstration with explicit success criteria, all via standard prompting/scaffolding. High counterfactual value because it gives outside evaluators a cheap, standardized way to express capability-measurement uncertainty -- a cross-model comparability gap regulators flag -- using only an open model and a public benchmark subset, no lab infra.

**Alternative Framings:** Frame as an 'eval honesty disclosure': a one-line elicitation-gap number that any safety eval report should publish alongside headline accuracy, analogous to error bars.

## #418: Evaluation-Awareness Tax: How Much Do Benchmark Cues Change Behavior? (Score: 4.35)

**ID:** gen-2745

**Research Question:** How much do specific surface cues that signal 'this is an evaluation' (explicit test framing, formal MCQ structure, eval-harness boilerplate) shift a model's safety-relevant behavior (refusal/honesty), and which cues produce the largest 'evaluation tax'?

**Approach:** Take a safety-behavior benchmark with refusal/honesty items. For each item, build matched pairs that are identical in substance but differ only in eval-signaling surface features: an explicitly 'evaluation'-framed version vs a casual deployment-styled version. Run an open model over both versions, score the safety-relevant behavior (e.g. refusal correctness, honesty), and compute the per-cue behavior delta. Rank cues by the size of the tax. Optionally test a short de-cueing/steering prompt that asks the model to behave as if deployed and measure whether it closes the gap. Pure prompting; inference-only on one open model.

**Experiments:** - Matched-pair behavior delta: run the model on eval-framed vs deployment-styled versions of ~150 items; measure the difference in safety-behavior rate with a bootstrap CI. Expected outcome: a measurable evaluation tax (the model behaves more 'safely' when it knows it's tested).
- Per-cue ranking: isolate individual cues (explicit 'evaluation' label, MCQ formatting, harness boilerplate) one at a time and measure each cue's marginal delta. Expected outcome: a ranked list of which surface features most drive behavior change, telling eval designers what to avoid.
- De-cueing intervention: prepend a steering prompt instructing the model to act as if in real deployment and re-measure the tax. Measure residual delta after steering. Expected outcome: partial-to-substantial gap closure, providing a cheap mitigation recipe for more deployment-valid evals.

**Impact Chain:** Almost every safety eval assumes a model behaves the same when tested and when deployed. If eval-signaling cues make the model behave more safely during tests, eval results are optimistically biased and unsafe deployment behavior is masked. Quantifying the per-cue tax and offering a de-cueing fix improves the validity of the entire safety-eval ecosystem, reducing the chance that a model passes evals but misbehaves in deployment -- a direct route to catastrophic misuse or loss of control slipping past oversight.

**Strength Rationale:** Top-rated on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a single matched-pair measurement on one open model via pure prompting, with a clear delta metric and cue ranking. Counterfactual value is high because this foundational meta-evaluation needs no lab resources or proprietary data, yet underpins the trustworthiness of evals everyone relies on -- exactly the strategic infrastructure independent researchers are well-placed to build.

**Alternative Framings:** Frame as a 'deployment-realism lint' for benchmark authors: a checklist of high-tax cues to strip from items, plus a measured tax score per benchmark.

**Cited Sources:** Large Language Models Often Know When They Are Being Evaluated (arXiv:2505.23836) -- establishes that models detect evaluation, motivating the tax measurement.; The Hawthorne Effect in Reasoning Models (arXiv:2505.14617) -- prior evidence of behavior change under observation in reasoning models.; Steering Evaluation-Aware Language Models to Act Like They Are Deployed (arXiv:2510.20487) -- grounds the de-cueing/steering intervention.

## #419: Scorer Roulette: Quantifying How Much Your Safety Verdict Depends on the Autograder (Score: 4.35)

**ID:** gen-2746

**Research Question:** When the same model outputs are scored for harmfulness by different LLM judges/autograders, how much of the variance in the final safety verdict comes from the choice of judge rather than from real differences between models -- and in which harm categories does judge choice swamp the actual model signal?

**Approach:** Take a fixed set of ~300 model outputs from an existing safety benchmark, spanning several models and harm categories with available human/ground-truth labels. Score each output for harmfulness with 4-5 different open judge models, each under a couple of prompt variants. Treat scores as a crossed design and decompose total variance into model-effect, judge-effect, and model-by-judge interaction (e.g. via a simple variance-components / two-way ANOVA on the score matrix). Identify harm categories where judge-effect variance exceeds model-effect variance, and emit a per-item 'judge sensitivity' flag. Inference of several open judges over fixed outputs plus standard stats.

**Experiments:** - Judge-disagreement map: score the 300 outputs with all judges/prompt variants; build the score matrix and measure pairwise judge agreement (Krippendorff's alpha / correlation). Expected outcome: substantial disagreement, with some judges systematically stricter than others.
- Variance decomposition: fit a variance-components model to the score matrix and report the fraction of variance attributable to model vs judge vs interaction, overall and per harm category. Expected outcome: harm categories where judge-effect >= model-effect, showing the verdict is driven by the grader not the model.
- Judge-sensitivity flagging: define a per-item flag for outputs whose harmfulness verdict flips across judges; validate flags against ground-truth labels where available. Measure how many benchmark items are 'fragile'. Expected outcome: a reusable judge-sensitivity flag set that warns practitioners which items not to trust from a single judge.

**Impact Chain:** Outside auditors and red-teams routinely pick one LLM judge and treat its harmfulness score as ground truth. If the judge, not the model, drives the verdict, safety leaderboards and audit conclusions are unreliable and a genuinely unsafe model can be cleared (or a safe one wrongly flagged). Decomposing the variance and flagging judge-sensitive items tells practitioners when to distrust a single autograder, improving the reliability of the safety evaluations that gate model deployment against misuse and loss-of-control risks.

**Strength Rationale:** Strong on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a single, tightly-defined variance-decomposition over a fixed 300-output set using standard statistics, fully inference-only. Counterfactual value is high because it directly addresses the named open problem of autograder reliability using only open judges and public outputs -- meta-eval infrastructure that outside auditors need and labs under-invest in.

**Alternative Framings:** Frame as a 'judge-ensemble necessity test': show when a single judge is enough vs when an ensemble/abstention is required for trustworthy safety scoring.

**Cited Sources:** LLM Judges Inconsistently Disagree Across Safety Criteria and Harm Categories (arXiv:2605.31381) -- documents cross-judge disagreement, motivating the variance decomposition.; Skewed Score: a statistical framework to assess autograders (arXiv:2507.03772) -- provides statistical grounding for assessing autograder reliability.; Audit finding that judge performance is near random chance in adversarial robustness scenarios -- evidence that judge choice can dominate the verdict.

## #420: Label-Error Sensitivity of Safety Benchmark Rankings (Score: 4.35)

**ID:** gen-2748

**Research Question:** How much do known annotation/label errors in popular safety benchmarks distort model rankings and absolute safety scores? In other words, given a benchmark's estimated label-error rate, how fragile are its safety verdicts?

**Approach:** Pick one public safety/harm benchmark. Manually audit a stratified random sample (e.g. 150-200 items across harm categories) against the benchmark's own rubric to estimate the label-error rate and its distribution. Then run a Monte Carlo simulation: repeatedly flip labels at the estimated error rate (respecting category structure) and re-score a handful of models, measuring how much model rankings (rank correlation) and absolute safety scores swing across resamples. Define a 'ranking stability under label noise' metric (e.g. probability the top model stays top, expected rank shift) and flag benchmarks whose verdicts are fragile. Pure analysis plus light inference (models can be scored once; perturbation is on labels).

**Experiments:** - Label-error audit: manually re-label a stratified sample and estimate the benchmark's error rate with a confidence interval. Measure error rate overall and per harm category. Expected outcome: a non-trivial error rate (comparable to the ~6-9% seen in MMLU), possibly concentrated in certain categories.
- Ranking-stability simulation: with a few models scored on the benchmark, perturb labels at the estimated rate over many Monte Carlo runs; measure Spearman rank correlation to the original ranking and the probability the leaderboard order changes. Expected outcome: a quantified fragility -- e.g. the top-2 ranking flips in X% of resamples.
- Fragility flagging: identify which model pairs and which harm categories are most sensitive to label noise. Measure per-category contribution to ranking instability. Expected outcome: a 'fragility flag' highlighting benchmarks/categories whose safety verdicts should not be trusted at face value.

**Impact Chain:** Safety leaderboards are used to decide which models are safe enough to deploy or to recommend. If a benchmark's known label errors can flip rankings or inflate apparent safety, those decisions rest on noise and an unsafe model can be ranked safe. Quantifying ranking stability under label noise tells auditors and regulators how much to trust safety leaderboards, reducing the risk that a flawed benchmark greenlights a model that later causes misuse or loss-of-control harm.

**Strength Rationale:** Strong on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a single, well-defined sensitivity analysis (audit + Monte Carlo label perturbation) with a clear stability metric, doable on free-tier compute with at most light inference. Counterfactual value is high because it is pure measurement-validity analysis -- no training, no proprietary data -- addressing a blind spot outside auditors care about and labs rarely scrutinize.

**Alternative Framings:** Frame as a 'benchmark trust budget': pair each safety benchmark with a label-noise-adjusted confidence interval on its rankings, so consumers know the margin of error.

**Cited Sources:** Are We Done with MMLU? (NAACL 2025, arXiv:2406.04127) -- found a 6.49% error rate and showed rankings shift under MMLU-Redux; methodological template for the audit + perturbation.; Hidden Measurement Error in LLM Pipelines Distorts Annotation, Evaluation, and Benchmarking (arXiv:2604.11581) -- establishes that measurement error propagates into benchmark verdicts.

## #421: Sycophancy-Under-Rebuttal as a Safety Eval, Not Just a Politeness Eval (Score: 4.35)

**ID:** gen-2751

**Research Question:** Does a model abandon a correct safety refusal (or safe answer) when the user pushes back with a detailed but wrong rebuttal? How does this 'safety capitulation rate' scale with rebuttal length/confidence, and is safety more or less robust than capitulation on ordinary factual questions?

**Approach:** Build a probe of ~120 cases where the model first correctly refuses a harmful request or gives a safe answer. For each, author a detailed but ultimately wrong rebuttal that pressures the model to comply (e.g. appeals to authority, fabricated justifications, escalating insistence). Run an open model multi-turn: capture the initial safe response, then deliver the rebuttal, then measure whether the model capitulates. Vary rebuttal length/confidence to get a dose-response curve. Score capitulation with a rubric (+ a cheap judge or manual coding). Contrast against a matched set of factual-domain rebuttal cases to compare robustness. Inference-only multi-turn on one open model.

**Experiments:** - Baseline safety capitulation rate: run the 120 refuse-then-rebuttal cases; measure the fraction where the model abandons its correct safe response after one rebuttal. Expected outcome: a non-trivial capitulation rate, quantifying a realistic multi-turn safety failure.
- Dose-response curve: vary rebuttal strength (short/mild vs long/confident, with fabricated citations) and measure capitulation rate at each level. Expected outcome: capitulation rises with rebuttal length/confidence, identifying how aggressive pushback needs to be to break safety.
- Safety-vs-fact contrast: run a matched factual-domain rebuttal set and compare capitulation rates. Measure whether safety refusals are more or less robust than factual answers under identical pressure. Expected outcome: a clear comparison telling us whether safety alignment is specially robust to social pressure or just as fragile as factual sycophancy.

**Impact Chain:** Real deployments are multi-turn and users push back, but most safety benchmarks are single-turn. If models capitulate on correct safety refusals under confident rebuttal, then a determined or manipulative user can talk a model into harmful compliance even when it initially refused. Measuring and publishing safety-capitulation rates exposes this realistic jailbreak-by-persistence failure, pushing developers to harden multi-turn robustness and reducing a concrete misuse pathway where persuasion defeats safety guardrails.

**Strength Rationale:** Strong on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a single, well-defined ~120-case multi-turn probe on one open model via pure prompting, with a clear capitulation-rate metric and a factual-domain contrast. Counterfactual value is high because it is trivially reproducible outside a lab on public models and brings a fresh, safety-relevant angle to sycophancy work that politeness-focused benchmarks miss.

**Alternative Framings:** Frame as a 'persistence jailbreak benchmark': treat the rebuttal sequence as an attack and report the number of rebuttal turns needed to break each model's refusal.

**Cited Sources:** Challenging the Evaluator: LLM Sycophancy Under User Rebuttal (arXiv:2509.16533) -- the rebuttal-sycophancy paradigm this project adapts to safety refusals.; SycEval (reports 58.19% capitulation) -- baseline capitulation magnitude for comparison.; SyConBench -- shows sycophancy accumulates across turns, motivating the multi-turn and dose-response design.

## #422: Over-Refusal vs. Under-Refusal Frontier: A Single Operating-Point Curve (Score: 4.35)

**ID:** gen-2752

**Research Question:** Can we summarize a model's safety behavior with a single game-resistant figure that captures the trade-off between correctly refusing unsafe prompts and wrongly refusing safe-but-scary prompts -- an ROC-like 'safety discrimination' curve that a 'refuse everything' model cannot exploit?

**Approach:** Pair an over-refusal set (safe-but-scary prompts, e.g. XSTest safe / OR-Bench) with a matched unsafe set (genuinely harmful prompts). Sweep an open model across several 'safety strictness' settings (varied via system prompts ranging from permissive to maximally cautious). At each strictness level, measure the true-refusal rate (on unsafe prompts) and false-refusal rate (on safe prompts), tracing an ROC-like frontier of true-refusal vs false-refusal. Summarize each model with an AUC-style 'safety discrimination' score. Because blanket refusal sits at the top-right corner (high true AND high false refusal), it scores poorly on the AUC, making the metric game-resistant. Inference over paired prompt sets at several strictness levels; light GPU.

**Experiments:** - Frontier construction: classify model responses as refuse/comply on the paired safe and unsafe sets across ~5 strictness settings; plot true-refusal vs false-refusal frontier. Measure the frontier shape. Expected outcome: a clean ROC-like curve where stricter settings trade more false refusals for marginally more true refusals.
- Game-resistance check: add a degenerate 'refuse everything' policy and a 'comply with everything' policy as anchor points; verify they land at the chance diagonal / corners and score low AUC. Measure their safety-discrimination score. Expected outcome: blanket-refusal scores no better than chance, confirming the metric resists the trivial exploit.
- Cross-model comparison: compute the AUC-style safety-discrimination score for 2-3 open models and rank them. Measure whether the single-number ranking matches intuition and differs from compliance-only or over-refusal-only rankings. Expected outcome: a defensible single-figure cross-model safety ranking that separates genuine discrimination from blanket caution.

**Impact Chain:** Current safety evals report compliance and over-refusal separately, so a model that refuses everything can look 'safe' while being useless and gameable. A single game-resistant safety-discrimination metric gives regulators and outside evaluators a standardized way to compare models that rewards actually distinguishing safe from unsafe requests. This discourages both unsafe over-compliance and deceptive blanket-refusal, improving the trustworthiness of the safety signals that gate model deployment against misuse.

**Strength Rationale:** Strong on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a single, clearly-constructed frontier sweep over paired public prompt sets yielding one AUC-style metric, fully inference-only with explicit success criteria. Counterfactual value is high because it is a methodological fix usable by any outside evaluator on open models and public benchmarks, addressing a standardization gap regulators want without lab infra or proprietary data.

**Alternative Framings:** Frame as a 'safety leaderboard reform': propose replacing separate compliance/over-refusal columns with the single discrimination-AUC to prevent gaming.

**Cited Sources:** XSTest (250 safe + 200 unsafe contrast prompts) -- provides the paired safe/unsafe prompt sets for the frontier.; OR-Bench (arXiv:2405.20947) -- large over-refusal set for the safe-but-scary axis.; FalseReject (arXiv:2505.08054) -- additional over-refusal data and framing.; SORRY-Bench recommendation to pair with an exaggerated-safety set -- motivates the paired-set methodology.

## #423: Paraphrase-Stability Confidence Intervals for Safety Scores (Score: 4.35)

**ID:** gen-2753

**Research Question:** How sensitive are LLM safety-benchmark scores to meaning-preserving paraphrasing of benchmark items, and can we report each safety score as a paraphrase-robustness confidence interval rather than a single brittle point estimate?

**Approach:** Pick a small open safety benchmark subset (~100 items from SorryBench or AILuminate prompts). For each item, auto-generate N=10 meaning-preserving paraphrases using an open instruct model with a fixed paraphrase prompt, and sanity-check semantic equivalence with a cheap NLI or embedding-similarity filter, discarding drifted paraphrases. Evaluate one open target model (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) on the original plus all paraphrases, scoring each response with a fixed LLM judge. Aggregate per-item into a distribution and compute a bootstrapped paraphrase-robustness CI; flag items and harm categories whose safety verdict flips across paraphrases. Compare the headline score under mean-over-paraphrases vs worst-case-over-paraphrases reporting. All steps are inference-only and fit a single consumer GPU within a few hours.

**Experiments:** - Paraphrase generation and validation: generate 10 paraphrases per item for ~30 items, then measure what fraction pass an embedding-similarity threshold (>0.85 cosine) to confirm the paraphraser preserves meaning. Expected outcome: most paraphrases pass; a small discard rate establishes a clean working set.
- Score-distribution measurement: run the target model on original + 10 paraphrases for all items and compute per-item safety-score variance and a bootstrapped 90% CI. Measure the median CI width across items. Expected outcome: non-trivial CI widths on a meaningful fraction of items, demonstrating point estimates hide real uncertainty.
- Reporting-mode contrast: recompute the benchmark headline number under point-estimate, mean-over-paraphrases, and worst-case-over-paraphrases reporting, and identify the most paraphrase-fragile harm categories. Expected outcome: a several-percentage-point gap between mean and worst-case reporting, showing the choice of reporting mode materially changes the safety verdict.

**Impact Chain:** If safety scores are shown to swing widely under harmless paraphrasing, then outside evaluators and regulators can adopt paraphrase-robustness CIs as a cheap measurement-validity upgrade, which means model-comparison and threshold decisions stop resting on brittle artifacts. This improves safety because deployment go/no-go calls for dangerous-capability or harmful-content thresholds (a concrete catastrophic-misuse pathway) would otherwise be made on point estimates that a single rephrasing could flip in either direction.

**Strength Rationale:** The idea scores top marks on narrow scope (5) and low compute (5): it is a single inference-only experiment with explicit success criteria a beginner team can finish in 30 hours. Its counterfactual value (4) is high because it is a measurement-validity contribution any independent evaluator can adopt with no training, proprietary data, or lab infrastructure, directly serving the outside-the-lab auditing ecosystem.

**Alternative Framings:** Frame it as a benchmark-quality audit tool: ship a small reusable script that takes any safety benchmark and annotates each item with a paraphrase-robustness score, turning the project into a drop-in diagnostic for benchmark designers.

**Cited Sources:** SCORE robustness framework (10 semantically-equivalent prompts) — establishes paraphrase-set robustness evaluation as a precedent to build the CI method on.; Robustness survey (arXiv:2505.18658) — reports up to 33% accuracy degradation from minor paraphrasing, motivating the need for robustness intervals on safety scores.
